title: FTS/LTC/CT/23/00012: Gavin Struthers v South Lanarkshire Council
text:
1

Decision of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) under
Section 17 of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland Local Taxation Chamber Rules
of Procedure 2022 (‘The Procedure Rules) and section 81 of the Local
Government Finance Act 1992 in relation to an Council Tax Finance/ Non List
appeal against a decision of a Local Authority.

Chamber Ref:  FTS/LTC/CT/23/00012

Re:1 Beechfield, Hawksland, Lesmahagow, Lanark, ML11 9PY
(“the dwelling”)

Parties:

Gavin Struthers, Moat Mains Farm, Lesmahagow, Lanark, ML11 9PY
(“the appellant”)

South Lanarkshire Council, Benefits and Revenue Services, PO Box 3591,
Glasgow, G73 9ED
(“the respondent”)

The First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) (“the tribunal”)

Tribunal Member:         Iain M MacRae (Legal Member)

Background

1.
The appellant appeals the decision of the respondent that from 1 April 2019 the
appellant was liable to pay council tax and an additional 100% council tax
charge as the dwelling had been unoccupied for more than 12 months.

Appeal to the First-tier Tribunal

2.
By letter dated 1 April 2022 the appellant served notice on the respondent
stating the matter by which and the grounds on which he was aggrieved. He
did so on the basis that the dwelling had been unoccupied since 2018/2019 and
could not be let or sold until a decision was reached by the court in an action
relating to access the property and sought repayment of all council tax payment
made since 2018/2019.  By letter dated 11 May 2022 the respondent notified
the appellant in writing that it believed the grievance was not well founded and
was unable to award an exemption. The appellant was still aggrieved and

2

lodged an appeal to the valuation appeal committee against the decision with
the respondent, as the levying authority, by letter dated 20 June 2022.  The
appellant has therefor complied with the requirements of section 81 of the Local
Government Finance Act 1992

3.
The appeal not having been withdrawn nor determined by the valuation appeal
committee by 1 April 2023 was transferred to the tribunal. The appellant
confirmed to the tribunal that he intended to proceed with the appeal and
requested a hearing. The respondent indicated that it was content for the
appeal to proceed based on the documents and written submission previously
lodged.

4.

The hearing

3

5.
A hearing was assigned for 10am on 28 June 2023. The appellant appeared on
his own behalf. The respondent was represented by Mr Bryan Robertson,
Policy, Appeals & Training Officer, South Lanarkshire Council.

6.
The appellant gave evidence. He relied on the documents lodged. He stated
that he now accepted that he was liable to pay council tax but that he did not
think it fair that he should have to pay the surcharge when the difficulty in letting
or selling the property were not of his own making.

7.
Mr Robertson for the respondent relied on the documents lodged and made
submission on behalf of the appellant.

Findings in Fact

8.
The tribunal found the following facts admitted or proved.

9.
That since 1975 the appellant has been the heritable proprietor of the dwelling.

10.
The dwelling has been unoccupied since 11 August 2016.

11.
On 19 May 2017 the appellant applied for an exemption from council tax liability
on that ground that the dwelling was unoccupied and undergoing major repair.

12.
The respondent granted the appellant’s application for exemption and the
dwelling was exempt from council tax from 11 August 2016 to 10 August 2017,
that maximum period permissible.

13.
From 11 August 2017 to 10 February 2018 the appellant was allowed a 50%
discount against the council tax liability as the dwelling was still unoccupied and
undergoing major repair. Six months was the maximum period allowable for this
discount.

14.
From 11 February 2018 to 31 March 2019 the appellant was allowed a 10%
unoccupied property discount against the council tax liability.

15.
With effect from 1 April 2019 the respondent’s policy on unoccupied properties
was that instead of being subject to a discount an increased amount of council
tax of 100% of the council tax was payable where properties have been
unoccupied for more than 12 months.

16.
As at the 1 April 2019 the dwelling had been unoccupied for more than 12
months and accordingly, was liable for payment of the an increased amount of
council tax of 100%.

4

Evidence and submissions
The Appellant
17.
When the case called the appellant accepted that he was liable to pay council
tax for the dwelling for the period from 1 April 2018. What he did not accept is
that he should be required to pay the surcharge, imposed as a consequence of
the property being unoccupied. He stated that he could not obtain landlord
insurance to allow him to let the property. He did not produce any evidence of
attempts to obtain landlord insurance.  He was unable to state whether having
landlord insurance was a pre-requisite of letting a property.
18.
He referred to the disposition and map. He accepted that the disposition
granted a right of access to the dwelling over two roads. He stated that one of
the two access roads to the dwelling had a cattle crossing and access along
that road could be restricted when the gates were open and cattle were
crossing.  That could be at any time of the day. He likened the cattle crossing
to a train level crossing. The other access road was blocked. He stated that the
property would not be attractive to tenants to rent due the muddy condition of
the road and perhaps the need to close gates due the cattle crossing.
Emergency vehicles might not be able to gain access.
19.
He said could not sell the property as there were ongoing legal proceedings
relating to the access. That case had been due to go to court but heads of
agreement to resolve the access dispute had been agreed. These had not yet
been formalised due to delays on the part of the other party.
20.
He accepted that the dwelling was capable of occupation. The appellant was
unable to point to any exception that would allow the respondent to make an
exception to the statutory provisions or the respondent’s policy in his favour. He
thought that the respondent should have the discretion to make an exception in
his favour. The dwelling was unoccupied through no fault of his.
The respondent
21.
Mr Robertson for the respondent relied on the respondent’s letter to the tribunal
dated 27 April 2023 which set out the background from when the property had
become unoccupied in August 2016. The appellant had been awarded an
exemption from 11 August 2016 to 10 August 2017; then a 50% discount from
11 August 2017 to 10 February 2018 (6 months being the maximum). Following
a telephone call from the appellant on 13 April 2018, a 10% unoccupied
property discount was awarded from 11 February 2018 to 31 March 2019. The
Council Tax (Variation for Unoccupied Dwellings) (Scotland) Regulations 2013
(the 2013 Regulations) empowered the respondent to modify the amount of

5

council tax payable for unoccupied properties. The appellant’s policy was that
from 1 April 2019 unoccupied properties were liable for an additional council
tax charge of 100%. This had been applied to the dwelling and was due by the
appellant. The appellant’s position to the respondent after that had been that
he could not get access or has limited or restricted access to the property, could
not obtain landlord insurance and could not sell or let the property until the
access dispute had been resolved.
Findings and Reasons
22.
The respondent has allowed the appellant all exemptions and discounts
available to the dwelling since it became unoccupied in August 2016. The
appellant’s argument at the appeal was that it was not his fault that the dwelling
remained unoccupied. That is not the test. The Council Tax (Exempt Dwellings)
(Scotland) Order 1997 (the 1997 Order) makes provisions for exempt
dwellings. The 2013 Regulations make provision for discounts in certain
circumstances.
23.
As at 1 April 2019 and indeed up to the date of the appeal the dwelling did not
match the definition of any of the classes of exempt dwelling specified in
Schedule 1 to the 1997 Order. So whilst the appellant had stated that the
dwelling would be difficult to let it was not an unoccupied dwelling (a) which
either formed part of premises which include another dwelling; or was situated
within the curtilage of another dwelling; (b) which is difficult to let separately
from that other dwelling; an (c) in respect of which a qualifying person has his
sole or main residence in that other dwelling. Paragraph 19 (Difficult to let
dwellings) did not therefor apply. Nor was it a dwelling (a) the occupation of
which is prohibited by law; or (b) which is kept unoccupied by reason of action
taken under powers conferred by or under any Act of Parliament, with a view to
prohibiting its occupation or to acquiring it.
24.
After the appellant had advised the responded that he could not let or sell the
property it had considered whether the court action meant that the property was
empty under statute or a difficult to let dwelling both as defined by the 1997
Order.  In the letter to the appellant dated 11 May 2022 the respondent had
correctly explained that it could not allow an exemption as the court action
relating to access did not prohibit occupation. The letter also explained that the
dwelling did not qualify for a difficult to let exemption as it the sat in its own land
with its own boundary and title and did not form part of another premises and
nor was it situated within the curtilage (or grounds) of another dwelling.
25.
The appellant had accepted in his evidence that the property was capable of
being occupied. There were two rights of access which could be enforced. The

6

appellant is not entitled to an exemption or discount simply because he
perceives that it may be difficult to let or sell the dwelling.
26.
As at the 1 April 2019 the appellant had exhausted all discounts available to
him. The dwelling was unoccupied; and had been unoccupied for a continuous
period exceeding 12 months. It had been continuously unoccupied more than
two years so there was no longer any scope for the respondent’s power to vary
the council tax to be restricted if the dwelling was being actively marketed for
sale or let.
27.
The respondent’s power contained in the 2013 Regulations to modify the
amount of council tax liability is limited so that the maximum amount of council
tax liability may not exceed an increase of 100%. That is amount they have
applied in terms of their policy. In reaching the decision that it did the
respondent has taken into account all of the relevant facts and circumstances
and has properly applied the legislation by which it is bound and has correctly
applied its own policy on unoccupied dwellings.
Decision

28.
The appeal is refused;

Right of Appeal

29.
In terms of Section 46 of the Tribunal (Scotland) Act 2014, a party
aggrieved by the decision of the Tribunal may appeal to the Upper
Tribunal for Scotland on a point of law only. Before an appeal can be made
to the Upper Tribunal, the party must first seek permission to appeal from
the First-tier Tribunal. That party must seek permission to appeal within
30 days of the date the decision was sent to them.

Iain M MacRae, Legal Member                 Date 13 July 2023

title: FTS/LTC/CT/23/00013: Carolyn Wallis v Stirling Council
text:
Decision of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) under
section 17 of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland Local Taxation Chamber (Rules of
Procedure) Regulations 2022 (‘The Procedure Rules’) and section 81 of the Local
Government Finance Act 1992 in relation to a Council Tax Finance appeal against a
decision of a Local Authority.

Chamber Ref: FTS/LTC/CT/23/00013

Re: 33 Birch Avenue, Stirling, FK8 2PL

(“the Property”)

Parties:

Carolyn Wallis

(“the Appellant”)

Stirling Council

(“the Local Authority”)

The First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber)
(“The Tribunal”)

Tribunal Member:   Mary Forbes (Legal Member)

Background

1. The Appellant lodged an appeal dated 15 February 2023 against the Local Authority’s
decision to not award a student exemption for council tax at the Property. The appeal is
being considered under section 81(1) of the Local Government Finance Act 1992.

Documents lodged with the Tribunal

2. In addition to the Appellant’s written submissions dated 15 February 2023 (received by
the Local Authority on 23 February 2023) and the Local Authority’s written submissions
dated 16 May 2023, the Tribunal was provided with the following documents:

a) the Appellant’s application for a student exemption;
b) a Student Certificate signed by the Finance Officer for the Onespirit Interfaith
Foundation dated 9 November 2022;

2

c) A spreadsheet showing the number of hours that the Appellant was expected to
study for her course;
d) Email correspondence between the Local Authority and the Appellant dated 8
December 2022, 22 December 2022, 12 January 2023, 17 January 2023, 18
January 2023, 6 February 2023 and 10 February 2023.

Hearing

3. This case called for a virtual hearing at 10am on 29 June 2023. The attendees were the
Appellant, the Legal Member, Gillian Taylor (Revenue and Benefits Manager for the
Local Authority) and Gillian Carr (Tribunal Clerk).

Decision

4. The Tribunal makes the following findings in fact:

a) The Appellant has been liable for the council tax payable in respect of the Property
from 5 June 2018.

b) Whilst studying for this course, the Appellant has continued to reside at the
Property.

c) The Appellant has been attending a Spiritual Development and Ministry Training
course at the OneSpirit Interfaith Foundation between 18 October 2021 and 22
July 2023.  This course requires the Appellant to undertake remote learning for
approximately 23 hours per week for at least 24 weeks in each academic year.

d) The OneSpirit Interfaith Foundation is an institution as defined in Schedule 3 of
The Council Tax (Discounts) (Scotland) Order 1992 (the ‘Order’).

e) On completion of the course, the Appellant will receive a certificate and be
ordained as an interfaith minister.

5. Having considered the material detailed at paragraph 2 above together with the oral
submissions from both the Appellant and the Local Authority at the Hearing, the Tribunal
dismisses the appeal for the following reasons:

a) In order to qualify for a student exemption from paying Council Tax, the Appellant
requires to meet the conditions set out in paragraph 6 of the Order.  Paragraph
6(1)(c) of the Order sets out the relevant test to be applied in the Appellant’s case.
This states that a student is a person who is -

(c) undertaking a course of education –

(i)
which is specified in Schedule 2 to this Order;

(ii)
which is provided by an institution specified in Schedule 3 to this Order;

3

(iii)
which he is required by the institution to attend for a period of at least
24 weeks within each academic year of the institution required to
complete the course; and
(iv)
in respect of which, in the opinion of the institution, a person would
ordinarily require to undertake periods of study or tuition (including any
periods of industrial, professional, or commercial experience
associated with the course which he requires to undertake to complete
the course) which amount, in the aggregate, to an average of at least
21 hours a week during the period mentioned in head (iii) above.

b) The Appellant meets the criteria set out in paragraph 6(1)(c)(ii)(iii) and (iv) of the
Order as set out above.  The Tribunal does not however consider, on the basis of
the evidence before it at the Hearing, that the Appellant’s studies can be
considered a ‘course of education’ as specified in Schedule 2 of the Order.

c) In respect of Schedule 2 of the Order, the Appellant’s primary argument was that
the course she was undertaking fell within the definition set out at paragraph 1(a)
as she was due to receive a certificate on completion in July 2023 which would
ordain her as an interfaith minister.  There was not however any documentation
provided to the Tribunal which evidenced either the nature of this certificate or
provided proof that the course qualified as a course at first degree or diploma level
as required by paragraph 1 of Schedule 2 of the Order.

d) A second argument put forward by the Appellant was that she was going to
undertake community work once ordained, and that this meant that the course fell
within the criteria set out in paragraph 5 of Schedule 2 to the Order.  Again, there
was no evidence before the Tribunal that the Appellant’s course was one of
undergraduate or postgraduate level as required by paragraph 5.  In addition, no
evidence was presented by the Appellant supporting her view that she would be
a form of community worker on completion of the course.

6. Right of Appeal

In terms of Section 46 of the Tribunal (Scotland) Act 2014, a party aggrieved by the
decision of the Tribunal may appeal to the Upper Tribunal for Scotland on a point of
law only. Before an appeal can be made to the Upper Tribunal, the party must first
seek permission to appeal from the First-tier Tribunal. That party must seek
permission to appeal within 30 days of the date the decision was sent to them.

……Mary Forbes……… Legal Member                 Date 5 July 2023

title: FTS/LTC/CT/23/00014: William Beaton & Sons v Ms Amy Beaton
text:
Decision of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) under
Section 17 of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland Local Taxation Chamber Rules of
Procedure 2022 (‘The Procedure Rules) and section 81 of the Local Government Finance
Act 1992 in relation to a Council Tax Finance/ Non List appeal against a decision of a
Local Authority.

Chamber Ref:  FTS/LTC/CT/23/00014

Re: Macrieston, Thornhill, Stirling, FK8 3QF

(“the Property”)

Parties: William Beaton & Sons, Macrieston, Thornhill, Stirling, FK8 3QF

(“the Appellant”)

Ms Amy Beaton,   (“the Appellant’s Representative”)

Stirling Council, Teith House, Kerse Road, Stirling, FK7 7QA

(“the Local Authority”)

The First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) (“the Tribunal”)

Tribunal Member:    Andrew McLaughlin

(Legal Member)

Background

[1] The Appellant appeals the decision of the Local Authority to increase their council tax
liability in respect of the Property by 100 per cent under The Council Tax (Variations for
Unoccupied Dwellings) (Scotland) Regulations 2013.

Documents lodged with the Tribunal

[2] The Tribunal had before it various emails exchanged between the parties regarding
the substance of the appeal together with various photographs and documents produced
by the Appellant. The Local Authority had also submitted written representations setting
out their opposition to the appeal. The Appellant had not submitted any clear statement
of the basis of the appeal and the Tribunal was left to clarify what exactly the Appellants
were basing their appeal on as a preliminary matter.

2

Hearing

[3] This case called for a hearing in Wallace House, Maxwell Place, Stirling at 10 am on 19
July 2023. The Appellant was represented by Ms Amy Beaton. The Local Authority was
represented by Ms Gillian Taylor.

[4] The Tribunal began by considering whether either party had any preliminary matters
to raise. Both parties confirmed that they did not and that they were content for the
Tribunal to commence hearing the appeal.

[5] The Tribunal established that the issue in dispute related to the Appellant’s
dissatisfaction at the decision of the Local Authority to increase their council tax liability
in respect of the Property by 100 per cent under The Council Tax (Variations for
Unoccupied Dwellings) (Scotland) Regulations 2013.

[6] Having heard from both parties and having considered the documentation before it,
the Tribunal made the following findings in fact:

Findings in Fact.

1. Under s 71 of the Local Government Finance Act 1992, the Appellant is liable to pay
council tax for the Property;

2. The Property was last occupied as a dwelling in or around 2004, by the mother of the two
brothers, Alan and Norman Beaton who are the current owners of the Property and
partners of the firm of William Beaton & Sons;

3. The Property is currently unoccupied and has been since 2004;

4. The Appellant has allowed the Property to fall into a state of disrepair since the last
occupant moved out;

5. Under Regulation 6 (2) (c) of The Council Tax (Variations for Unoccupied Dwellings)
(Scotland) Regulations 2013, the Local Authority has increased the council tax in respect
of the Property by 100 per cent on account of it having been unoccupied for over a year;

6. The Local Authority has correctly applied the law and has made its decision after assessing
all of the relevant facts and considering and discounting any possible exemptions that
might otherwise have been applicable.

Note:-

3

[7] This appeal had no merit in it. Nothing was put to the Tribunal that suggested that the
Local Authority had not applied the law correctly.

[8] The Appellant made reference to the Property being an ‘agricultural holding’ but there
was no dispute that the Property was entered on the council tax valuation list.  The Local
Authority had considered whether the Property could be eligible for an exemption under
Regulation 14 of Schedule 1 of the Council Tax (Exempt Dwellings) (Scotland) Order 1997.

[9] They had concluded that it was not, as it is clearly not used for agricultural purposes
only.  The Property had been a private home which had been allowed to fall into a state of
disrepair. It was adjacent to a busy builder’s yard operated by the Respondents which
was their main place of business.

[10] Much of the Appellant’s argument was focused on the imposition of the council tax
premium as being “unfair”. However, the Tribunal requires to apply the law and an
individual’s own perception of what may or may not be fair is irrelevant.

[11] Having made the above findings and having adjourned to consider matters, the
Tribunal refuses the Appeal.

Right of Appeal

In terms of Section 46 of the Tribunal (Scotland) Act 2014, a party aggrieved by the
decision of the Tribunal may appeal to the Upper Tribunal for Scotland on a point of
law only. Before an appeal can be made to the Upper Tribunal, the party must first seek
permission to appeal from the First-tier Tribunal. That party must seek permission to
appeal within 30 days of the date the decision was sent to them.

Andrew McLaughlin

title: FTS/LTC/CT/23/00015: Don Cameron v Glasgow City Council
text:
Decision of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) under
Section 17 of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland Local Taxation Chamber Rules
of Procedure 2022 (‘The Procedure Rules) and section 81 of the Local
Government Finance Act 1992 in relation to a Council Tax Finance/ Non List
appeal against a decision of a Local Authority.

Chamber Ref:  FTS/LTC/CT/23/00015

Re: 3 Kelburne Gardens, Baillieston, Glasgow G69 7BD (“the Property”)

Parties:

Don Cameron, 9 Linlithgow Gardens, Glasgow G32 0TR (“the Appellant”)

Glasgow City Council, City Chambers, George Square, Glasgow G2 1DU (“the
Local Authority”)

The First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) (“the Tribunal”)

Tribunal Member: Richard Mill (Legal Member)

Background

1. The Appellant challenges the decision of the respondent in respect of the Council
Tax liability for the property for the period 22 June 2022 until 4 August 2022.

2. The Tribunal has determined that it is appropriate to make a decision based on
written representations, without a hearing, in terms of Rule 9 of the First-tier
Tribunal for Scotland Local Taxation Chamber (Rules of Procedure) Regulations
2022 as, amended.

Documents lodged with the Tribunal

3. Both parties have produced formal written submissions together with relevant
supporting documentation and additional emails.

Findings and reasons

4. The Tribunal was satisfied that it had sufficient evidence before it to reach a fair
determination of the appeal.

5. The property is 3 Kelburne Gardens, Baillieston, Glasgow G69 7BD.  The property
was formerly owned by the Appellant’s mother who died on 20 August 2021.

6. The Appellant was appointed as the sole executor to his late mother’s estate by
way of a grant of Confirmation issued by the Commissariot, Glasgow and
Strathkelvin dated 22 December 2021.  He did not receive notice of the
Confirmation until 5 February 2022.

7. Schedule 1 of the Council Tax (Exempt Dwellings) (Scotland) Order 1997 specifies
the category of properties which are exempt properties, which includes those
specified in Section 6:-

A dwelling—

(a)
which is not the sole or main residence of any person; and

(b)
in respect of which any liability to pay council tax (but for the terms of
this Order) would fall to be met solely out of the estate of a deceased
person and either—

(i)
no grant of confirmation to the estate of that person has been
made; or

(ii)
no more than 6 months have passed since such a grant was
made.

8. The Local Authority applied the provisions of Section 6 of the 1997 Order for the
6 month period commencing with the date of the said Confirmation ie 22 December
2021, ending on 22 June 2022.

9. The Appellant complains that the 6 month period of exemption should run from the
date that he received notice of the Confirmation and not from the date of
Confirmation itself. This is acknowledged to be contrary to the statutory provision
but the Appellant generally submits that this should happen out of natural fairness.
He does not rely upon any statutory or other legal basis for this. He submits that
the legislation is ‘flawed” but his personal views regarding the terms and effect of
the statutory provisions are irrelevant.

10. It is unfortunate that the Appellant did not receive notice of the Confirmation for
some 6 weeks after it was issued.  There is however no provision in the 1997 Order
to accommodate a delayed period between Confirmation being granted and notice
provided to an executor.  If Parliament had intended for such a provision or other
right of relief then it would be found within the Order but it is not. The Local Authority

title: FTS/LTC/CT/23/00016: Martin Faulds
text:
Decision of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) under
Section 17 of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland Local Taxation Chamber Rules
of Procedure 2022 (‘The Procedure Rules) and section 81 of the Local
Government Finance Act 1992 in relation to an Council Tax Finance/ Non List
appeal against a decision of a Local Authority.

Chamber Ref:  FTS/LTC/CT/23/00016

Re:
99 McLaren Crescent, Glasgow, G20 0LD (“the Property”)

Parties:

Martin Faulds, 99 McLaren Crescent, Glasgow, G20 0LD (“the Appellant”)

Glasgow City Council, City Chambers, George Square, Glasgow G2 1DU (“Local
Authority”)

The First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) (“the Tribunal”)

Tribunal Member:  Nicola Irvine (Legal Member)

1.      Background

1.1
The Appellant appeals the decision of the Local Authority to find him liable to
pay council tax in respect of the Property and to apply for a Summary Warrant
in respect of that liability.

1.2
In terms of section 81(1) of the Local Government Finance Act 1992, the
Appellant is entitled to appeal to the Tribunal if he is aggrieved by a decision of
a local authority that a dwelling is a chargeable, or that he is liable to pay council
tax in respect of such a dwelling. The Appellant was notified in writing by the
Local Authority that it believed that his grievance was not well founded. The
section 81 conditions have been met.

2.      Documents lodged with the Tribunal.

2.1   Email from the Appellant dated 19 April 2023.
2.2   Email from the Appellant to the Local Authority dated 2 August 2022.
2.3   Email from the Local Authority to the Appellant dated 29 June 2022.
2.4   Written submissions from the Local Authority.
2.5   List of Authorities for the Local Authority.

3.
Consideration of the Appeal

3.1
The parties agreed that a hearing was not required and that the appeal could
be dealt with by written representations. The Tribunal determined that it is
appropriate to dispose of the appeal by written representations in terms of rule
9(3) of the Procedure Rules. The issue before the Tribunal was whether the
Local Authority was entitled to apply for a summary warrant in relation to the
Appellant’s council tax liability and to apply a 10% surcharge.

4.
Findings in fact

4.1
The Appellant was liable to pay council tax in respect of the property from 10
May 2016 to 30 June 2016 and from 11 December 2017 to 22 March 2018.

4.2
The notice of appeal was served on the Local Authority prior to 1 April 2023
and has not been withdrawn or otherwise disposed of.

5.
Decision with reasons

5.1
The Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

5.2
There was no material from the Appellant to suggest that he disputed liability to
pay council tax for the periods 10 May 2016 to 30 June 2016 and 11 December
2017 to 22 March 2018.

5.3
The issue for the Appellant is whether the Local Authority was entitled to apply
for a Summary Warrant and apply a 10% surcharge to the liability.

5.4
The email from the Local Authority to the Appellant dated 29 June 2022 sets
out that the Appellant reached agreement with the Local Authority’s collection
agent in 2019 to pay off his outstanding council tax liability at that time. There
is no material from the Appellant to contradict that. The email from the Local
Authority narrates that further council tax bills were issued to the Appellant on
12 October 2021 and that the sums due were not paid within the required time.
Again, there is no material from the Appellant to contradict that.

5.5
In terms of paragraph 2(2) of Schedule 8 to the Local Government Finance Act
1992, the Local Authority is entitled to apply for a Summary Warrant authorising
recovery of the sum remaining due along with a surcharge of 10%.

6. Right of Appeal

In terms of Section 46 of the Tribunal (Scotland) Act 2014, a party aggrieved by
the decision of the Tribunal may appeal to the Upper Tribunal for Scotland on a
point of law only. Before an appeal can be made to the Upper Tribunal, the party
must first seek permission to appeal from the First-tier Tribunal. That party must
seek permission to appeal within 30 days of the date the decision was sent to
them.

Nicola Irvine

title: FTS/LTC/CT/23/0017: Marble Properties Ltd v And Renfrewshire Council
text:
1

Decision of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) under
Section 17 of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland Local Taxation Chamber Rules
of Procedure 2022 (‘The Procedure Rules) and section 81 of the Local
Government Finance Act 1992 in relation to an Council Tax Finance/ Non List
appeal against a decision of a Local Authority.

Chamber Ref:  FTS/LTC/CT/23/0017

Re:
2/1 25 Lawn Street, Paisley, PA1 1HD

(“the dwelling”)

Parties:

Marble Properties Ltd, 9 Harmony Place, Glasgow, G51 3SF (“the appellant”)

And

Renfrewshire Council, Renfrewshire House, Cotton Street, Paisley, PA1 1JD

(“the respondent”)

The First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) (“the Tribunal”)

Background

1.
The appellant appeals the decision of the respondent of 10 April 2018 that the
dwelling was an exempt dwelling from 25 January 2016 to 24 January 2017 as
""Incapable of Habitation" and that from 25 January 2017 to 4 October 2017 it
was a "Long term empty property" entitling the appellant to a 10% reduction in
council tax liability.

Appeal to the First-tier Tribunal

2.
The decision notice is dated 10 April 2018. On 18 April 2018 the appellant
served notice on the respondent stating the matter by which and the grounds
on which it was aggrieved. It did so on the basis that it believed that the dwelling
should be considered as a dwelling that is empty under statute, where
occupation of which is prohibited by law; or which is kept unoccupied by reason
of action taken under powers conferred by or under any Act of Parliament, with
a view to prohibiting its occupation or to acquiring it. Furthermore, the appellant
sought the exemption to be applied for the period 28 March 2016 to 4 October
2017. By email dated 14 May 2018 the respondent notified the appellant in
writing that it believed the grievance was not well founded. The appellant was

2

still aggrieved then lodged an appeal to the valuation appeal committee against
the decision with the respondent, as the levying authority, on 11 June 2018.
The appellant has therefor complied with the requirements of section 81 of the
Local Government Finance Act 1992 (the “1992 Act”).

3.

committee by 1 April 2023 was transferred to the tribunal. The appellant
confirmed to the tribunal that it intended to proceed with the appeal and
requested a hearing. The respondent indicated that it was content for the
appeal to proceed based on the written submission previously lodged.

The hearing

5.
A WebEx hearing was assigned for 10am on 21 June 2023. On 20 June 2023
the respondent advised that they would not be represented at the hearing of
the appeal but wished the appeal to proceed on the basis of the documents and

6.

7.
Mr Wong gave evidence and made submission on behalf of the appellant.

Findings in Fact.

8.
The Tribunal found the following facts admitted or proved.

9.
That from 2009 the appellant was the heritable proprietor of the dwelling.

10.
The dwelling forms part of a tenement consisting of six flats, two of which are
shops.

11.
From 2009 to 2016 the appellant experienced difficulty in obtaining agreement
from the other flat owners to allow mutual repairs to the tenement, including
repairs to the roof, to be undertaken.

12.
That following an inspection of the dwelling by the respondent on 20 January
2016 the owners of the flats comprising the tenement were issued a “disrepair
letter” by the respondent requiring repairs to prevent water ingress.

13.
By letter from the respondent to the appellant dated 2 March 2016 the
respondent referred to the letter of 20 January 2016 and stated that due to the
level of dampness recorded in the dwelling it was not of tolerable standard as

4

defined by the Housing (Scotland) Act 1987 (as amended) and should not be
inhabited until the defects causing the rain water ingress were rectified.

14.
That up to 27 March 2016 the tenant of the dwelling was liable to pay the council
tax.

15.
The dwelling was last occupied on 27 March 2016.

16.
That from 28 March 2016 to 4 October 2017 the appellant is liable to pay the
council tax due for the dwelling.

17.
During the period 28 March 2016 to 4 October 2017 the occupation of dwelling
was not prohibited by law; nor kept unoccupied by reason of action taken under
powers conferred by or under any Act of Parliament, with a view to prohibiting
its occupation or to acquiring it.

18.
From the 28 March 2016 the dwelling was an unoccupied dwelling which was
undergoing or had undergone (since the last occupation day) major repair work
to render it habitable.

19.
The major repair work undertaken was repairs to the roof to make the dwelling
watertight and then internal work to rectify the damage caused by the ingress
of water over a period of years.

20.
The major repair work in question was substantially completed sometime
between 21 October 2016 and 4 October 2017.

21.
After the major repair work in question was substantially completed the dwelling
remained unoccupied until 4 October 2017.

The legislation

22.
Council Tax (Exempt Dwellings) (Scotland) Order 1997

3. Exempt dwellings

The classes of dwelling specified in Schedule 1 to this Order are prescribed as
exempt dwellings for the purposes of section 72(6) of the Act.

Schedule 1 EXEMPT DWELLINGS

Para 2 Dwellings under repair
2.
An unoccupied dwelling–
(a)  which–
(i)  is undergoing or has undergone (since the last occupation day) major
repair work to render it habitable; or

5

(ii)  is undergoing or has undergone (since the last occupation day)
structural alteration;
(b)  in respect of which no more than 12 months have elapsed since the
last occupation day; and
(c)  in respect of which no more than 6 months have elapsed since the
major repair work or structural alteration in question was substantially
completed.

Para 7 Dwellings empty under statute

7.
A dwelling–
(a)  the occupation of which is prohibited by law; or
(b)  which is kept unoccupied by reason of action taken under powers
conferred by or under any Act of Parliament, with a view to prohibiting
its occupation or to acquiring it.

The evidence & submissions

The appellant

23.
Mr Wong gave evidence on behalf of the appellant. He stated that there had
been tenants in the dwelling. He gave details of the difficulties he had
experienced over a number of years of trying to have the owners of the other
flats in the tenement agree to repairs to the roof. He had taken it upon himself
to have repairs carried out but these had been ineffectual. It was only after the
respondent issued their disrepair notice that he had managed to have factors
appointed and the repairs to the roof were then undertaken. These were
competed by 21 July 2016 but, due to years of concealed water penetration the
fabric of the building was saturated and it required dehumidifying and then
further work to bring the dwelling back up to a habitable condition. Mr Wong
said it had taken months and months to dry out the dwelling after the water
ingress had been stopped. After the fabric of the building had dried out further
repairs were carried out. He said the other work was not completed and the
dwelling did not become habitable until 4 October 2017. New tenants moved in
on the 5 October 2017.

24.
Mr Wong gave evidence that following on from the inspection on the 20 January
2016 the tenants remained in occupation of the dwelling. They had told him that
they had been in touch with Shelter for advice and that if they were forced to
leave they would go back to Shelter and Citizens Advice Scotland.  Mr Wong
explained that he was aware that tenants could not be removed from a dwelling
without a court order. He had no idea on what basis the respondent had stated,
in their submissions to the tribunal, that the dwelling had been vacated by the
tenants on 24 January 2016. He referred to his email to the respondent of 14
April 2018 where he stated.

“With regards to the last occupation date of the previous tenant, neither
you or I can confirm an exact date as they refused to meet to check out

6

and return the properly plus keys to me until 27.03.2016. I ended their
tenancy accordingly reflecting that.

25.
In evidence he stated that he was unsure whether the respondent’s view was
based on something the tenants had told them or other information. He stated
that tenants can be difficult and are not always truthful. He gave clear evidence
that the tenants did not move out of the dwelling until he met them there on 27
March 2016 and when he witnessed them removing belongings. It was from
then that dwelling had become unoccupied.

26.
Mr Wong did not think it was fair that the appellant had to pay council tax whilst
the dwelling was uninhabitable. It was his position that the dwelling was
uninhabitable until the 4 October 2017 the day before it became occupied by
tenants. He felt it was unfair that the respondent only allowed the appellant a
10% discount during the period the dwelling was a “long term empty property”
The respondent had the power to allow discount of between 10 and 50%. He
felt that, given the money the appellant had spent on trying to effect repairs and
the difficulties the appellant had in engaging the other flat owners the appellant
should have been entitled to a larger discount than the minimum.

The respondent

27.
The respondent relied on the documents lodged and their written submissions.
These referred to the disrepair letter dated 20 January 2016 but that letter was
not produced. The submissions referred to the subsequent letter dated 2 March
2016 which stated the dwelling

“currently fails the Tolerable Standards as defined in the Housing
(Scotland) Act 1987 (as amended) and should not be inhabited until the
defects casing the rain water ingress are rectified.”

28.
The respondent’s summary of facts referred to the dwelling being vacated by
the tenants on 24 January 2016. They then gave details of the exemption and
then the discount allowed. The exemption applied from 25 January 2016 but
could last no longer that 12 months from the day after date they said the
property was last occupied.  This meant that, regardless of the date from when
the appellant took possession back (and became liable for council tax) the
exemption could last only to 24 January 2017. The appellant had the benefit of
the exemption from 27 March 2016 through to 24 January 2017. From 25
January 2017 to 4 October 2017 a 10% long terms empty property discount
was applied. The policy of the respondent was to allow a discount of 10%.

Findings and reasons

29.
An area of dispute between the parties was at what date the dwelling was last
occupied. Mr Wong had raised this issue in his email to the respondent of 14
April 2018. He gave unchallenged evidence, which the tribunal accepted, that
it was not until the 27 March 2016 that the tenants had completed the process

7

of moving themselves and their belongings out of the dwelling, on which date
they then surrendered the dwelling back to the appellant.  The respondent had
made a bare assertion of fact, that the tenants had vacated the dwelling on 24
January 2016 but gave no indication as to what information or circumstances
had led them to conclude that the dwelling was last occupied on 24 January
2016.

30.
The question for the tribunal is not when the appellant took possession of the
dwelling back, as the exemption can only last for a maximum of 12 months from
after the dwelling was last occupied, not from when the appellant managed to
regain possession. However, in the absence of evidence from the respondent,
the only certainty is that the dwelling was occupied up to 27 March 2016 and
so unoccupied from 28 March 2016.

31.
The major repair work to render the dwelling habitable did not consist of only
repairs to the roof but also repairing the damage caused by water penetration.
As a consequence, work carried on after the roof repairs were completed on 21
July 2016. The tribunal was not prepared to accept Mr Wong’s assertion that
this work was only substantially completed on the 4 October 2017 and that the
very next day a tenant was found. That said Mr Wong did not impress as the
kind of person who would have allowed the dwelling to remain unoccupied for
longer than was necessary as to do so would have denied the appellant rental
income. The work may not have been finally completed until the day before the
tenant moved in but on balance it was more likely that it had been substantially
completed before that.

32.
However nothing turns on this. Based on Mr Wong’s evidence, which was
accepted, it had taken several months to dry out the dwelling. It was only after
the dwelling had been dehumidified that the work to finalise the major repairs
to render it habitable could be undertaken. Even if that work could have been
completed within 3 months of the roof repairs being finished, on balance, it was
likely that the work as a whole, was not substantially complete until sometime
after 21 October 2016 but before 5 October 2017.

33.
The dwelling had, since the last occupation day, been undergoing or had
undergone major repair work to render it habitable and as such was an exempt
dwelling. The exemption could last for no more than 12 months from after the
last occupation day. Where the work is substantially completed the exemption
can still apply, if the dwelling remains unoccupied, but for no more than 6
months after the major repair work is substantially completed. So had the
appellant substantially completed the works in 3 months from the last
occupation date and the dwelling remained unoccupied, the total period of
exemption that could have been applied would have been 9 months. The period
of up to 6 month allowable after the substantial completion of the works cannot
extend the overall limit of 12 months.

34.
As the works were not substantially completed until sometime after 21 October
2016 it matters not whether the repairs were substantially completed on 22
October 2016 or 4 October 2017 or any day in between. If the repairs were not

8

substantially completed until the 4 October 2017 the dwelling is only exempt for
a maximum of 12 months from the day after it was last occupied so from 28
March 2016 to 27 March 2017. On the other hand if the repairs were
substantially completed by the 22 October 2017 and as the dwelling remained
unoccupied the exemption continued for a period of no more than 6 months up
to the 27 March 2017 at the latest. Either way the appellant is entitled to the full
12 months exemption which was what the respondent had allowed. The only
difference being the date from which that exemption applies.

35.
The letter from the respondent to the appellant dated 2 March 2016 stating that
the dwelling “failed the Tolerable Standard…” was apt to confuse. The letter
stated that the dwelling “should not” rather than “must not” be inhabited.  The
dwelling not being of a tolerable standard would no doubt have caused difficulty
in selling or letting it. However there is no separate exemption for dwellings that
do not meet the tolerable standard.

36.
It did not follow from that letter that the occupation of the dwelling was prohibited
by law or the dwelling was being kept unoccupied by reason of action taken
under powers conferred by or under any Act of Parliament, with a view to
prohibiting its occupation or to acquiring it. As such the appellant are not entitled
to an exemption under paragraph 7 of The Council Tax (Exempt Dwellings)
(Scotland) Order 1997 which would not have been time limited.

37.
The Appellant thought that it was unfair that a long term empty property
discount of only a 10% was allowed. Whilst the responded does have the power
decide on the level of discount, their policy was to offer only a fixed 10%
discount. It is not the function of this Tribunal to examine the lawfulness of that
policy. As the respondent had applied their policy the appellant is only entitled
to a discount of 10% over the period of 28 March to 4 October 2017 during
which the dwelling was a long term empty property.

Decision

38.
The appeal is allowed; the decision notice of the respondent dated 10 April
2016 together with the council tax notices and calculation of the amount
payable as council tax and water charges by the appellant during the period 28
March 2016 to 4 October 2017 are quashed; and in terms of in terms of rule
38(4) the respondent  is ordered to re-calculate the amount which the appellant
is liable to pay to the respondent  in respect of council tax and water charges,
and issue a demand to the appellant for that amount, on the basis that the
dwelling was last occupied on 27 March 2017; that from 28 March 2016 to 27
March 2017 the dwelling was an exempt dwelling for the purposes of section
72 of the Local Government Finance Act 1992; and that from 28 March to 4
October 2017 the dwelling was a long term empty property entitling the
appellant to a 10% reduction in council tax liability over that period.

Right of Appeal

9

37.
In terms of Section 46 of the Tribunal (Scotland) Act 2014, a party
aggrieved by the decision of the Tribunal may appeal to the Upper
Tribunal for Scotland on a point of law only. Before an appeal can be made
to the Upper Tribunal, the party must first seek permission to appeal from
the First-tier Tribunal. That party must seek permission to appeal within
30 days of the date the decision was sent to them.

Background

1.
The appellant appeals the decision of the respondent of 7 December 2017 that
the appellant was liable to pay the council tax for the dwelling located at 18

Appeal to the First-tier Tribunal

2.
On receipt of the decision the appellant served notice on the respondent stating
the matter by which and the grounds on which the appellant was aggrieved. It
did so on the basis that since 23 November 2017 there had been tenants who
were occupying the dwelling who should be liable for payment of the council
tax. The respondent then notified the appellant in writing that they believed the
grievance was not well founded. The appellant was still aggrieved and lodged
an appeal to the valuation appeal committee against the decision with the

Findings in Fact.

9.
The tribunal found the following facts admitted or proved:

10.

The legislation

11.
Local Government Finance Act 1992

Section 76.— Liability in prescribed cases.

(1)  Subsections (3) and (4) below shall have effect in substitution for section
75 above in relation to any chargeable dwelling of a class prescribed for the
purposes of this subsection.

(2)  Subsections (3) and (4) below shall have effect in substitution for section
75 above in relation to any chargeable dwelling of a class prescribed for the
purposes of this subsection, if the levying authority so determines in relation to

(3)  Where on any day this subsection has effect in relation to a dwelling, the
owner of the dwelling shall be liable to pay the council tax in respect of the
dwelling and that day.

4

(4)  Where on any day two or more persons fall within subsection (3) above,
they shall each be jointly and severally liable to pay the council tax in respect
of the dwelling and that day.

(5)  Subsection (4) of section 75 above shall apply for the purposes of
subsection (4) above as it applies for the purposes of subsection (3) of that
section.

(6)  Regulations prescribing a class of chargeable dwellings for the purposes
of subsection (1) or (2) above may provide that, in relation to any dwelling of
that class, subsection (3) above shall have effect as if for the reference to the

(7)  Subsection (7) of section 72 above shall apply for the purposes of

The Council Tax (Liability of Owners)(Scotland) Regulations 1992

2.

Para 3

each of whom–
(a) is a tenant of, or has a licence to occupy, part only of the dwelling;

The evidence & submissions

13.
Mr Wong gave evidence and made submission on behalf of the appellant. He
referred to the letter dated 4 December 2017 in which the tenants had accepted
they were occupying the dwelling and asked the respondent to issue the council
tax demand in their names. The appellant maintained that the occupiers of the
dwelling should be liable. Mr Wong submitted that at some time after the
tenants had taken up occupation the two households had become one
household. That had been accepted by the respondent and as a consequence
the appellant’s liability to pay the council tax had ended on 28 January 2019.
Mr Wong suggested that the tenants may have been one household much
earlier but no evidence was led to support that contention. Mr Wong for the

5

appellant confirmed the facts found as proved at paragraph 5.1 above were not
in dispute.

14.
The responds relied on their written submissions. The submissions refer to the
dwelling being classed as a house of (sic) multiple occupation if each person
who lives in it is a tenant able to occupy only part of the dwelling. The
submission identified that both tenants held separate tenancy agreements for
specific rooms and as a consequence the appellant and not the residents was
liable for the council tax. The submissions referred to The Council Tax (Liability
of Owners) (Scotland) Regulations 1992 (as amended). The consequence of
the application of Schedule 1, Para 3 was that the appellant not the occupiers
were liable for the council tax.

Findings and reasons

15.
The facts were not in dispute and it is clear that as at the 23 November 2017
the dwelling was occupied, by two persons who did not constitute a single
household each of whom was a tenant of part only of the dwelling. The
respondent had identified and applied the correct test set out in Paragraph 3 of
Schedule 1 of the 1992 regulations to the facts. The dwelling was therefor one
of the classes of dwelling prescribed for the purposes of section 76(1) of the
1992 Act.  As a consequence the respondent was correct to decide that, as a
matter of law, it was the appellant, as owner of the dwelling and not the tenants
as occupiers who was liable to pay the council tax. How the tenants and
appellant dealt with that between themselves would have been a private matter
between themselves.

16.
What the appellant and tenants could not do is, by agreement, circumvent or
opt-out of the terms of the legislation and require the respondent to issue the
council tax demands in the names of the tenants. The tenants’ letter dated 4
December 2017 was of no effect and could not have been acted upon by the
respondent. The question for the tribunal was whether at the date of the
decision it was correct. It was not a matter for the Tribunal to determine on what
day after 23 November 2017 the occupiers became members of the same
household and so liable to pay the council tax.

Decision

17.
The Appeal is refused.

Right of Appeal

18.
In terms of Section 46 of the Tribunal (Scotland) Act 2014, a party
aggrieved by the decision of the Tribunal may appeal to the Upper
Tribunal for Scotland on a point of law only. Before an appeal can be made
to the Upper Tribunal, the party must first seek permission to appeal from

6

the First-tier Tribunal. That party must seek permission to appeal within
30 days of the date the decision was sent to them.

title: FTS/LTC/CT/23/00019: Mr Donald Mitchell v Renfrewshire Council (Levying Authority
text:
Decision of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) under Rule
17 and 34 of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland Local Taxation Chamber Rules of
Procedure 2022 (“the Procedure Rules”) and section 81 of the Local Government
Finance Act 1992 in relation to a Council Tax Finance/ Non List appeal against a
decision of a Local Authority

Chamber Ref: FTS/LTC/CT/23/00019

Re: 02/01 16 Station Road, Renfrew, PA4 8RP (“the Property”)

Parties:

Mr Donald Mitchell (“the Appellant”)

Renfrewshire Council (Levying Authority) (“the Respondent”)

The First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) (“the Tribunal”)

Tribunal Member: James Bauld (Legal Member)

Background

1. This appeal bears to be an appeal in respect of liability for council tax and appears to
be proceeding under section 81 of the Local Government Finance Act 1992 (“the
1992 Act”)

2. The appellant’s complaints do not actually relate to the amount of council tax which
has been levied but in respect to the water and sewerage charges which are included
in the annual council tax notice

3. Water and sewerage charges are not part of the council tax levied by local authorities.
They are separate charges under and in terms of the Water Industry (Scotland) Act
2002 (“the 2002 Act”)

4. Since the 2002 Act was introduced, the manner of demanding and recovering of
water and sewerage charges for liable persons has been set out in a number of
statutory instruments.

5. The initial regulations were contained in The Water Services Charges (Billing and
Collection) (Scotland) Order 2010 (“the 2010 Order”) and subsequently  in a series
of statutory instruments called Water and Sewerage Services to Dwellings (Collection
of Unmetered Charges by Local Authority) (Scotland) Orders (“the Collection Orders”)
Orders bearing this title have been made in 2014, 2017, 020 and 2023..

6. Each of these orders set out a process whereby a local authority issues demands for
payments of the water and sewerage services being levied by Scottish Water to
dwellings within the local authority areas. The regulations also give the local authority
the power to recover these charges on behalf of Scottish Water

7. Within each set of regulations is a provision allowing appeal by any person aggrieved
by the decision of a local authority in respect of the water and sewerage charges
being levied in respect of any property. This appeal therefore properly proceeds
under those Regulations starting with the 2010 Order and continuing through the
various Collection Orders.

Documents lodged with the Tribunal.

8. the Appellant lodged:

(a) Copy of Regulation 4 of The Water and Sewerage Charges (Exemption and
Reduction)(Scotland)Regulations 2006;
(b) Copy of Regulations 13 and 79 of The Council Tax Reduction (Scotland)
Regulations 2021;
(c) Council Tax claim receipts dated 30 November 2018 and 14 February 2019;
(d) Universal Credit statements for July 2019 and from August 2019 to December
2022;
(e) Universal Credit Work Capability Assessment decision letter dated 25
February 2020;
(f) Email correspondence dated 9 and 13 March 2023; and
(g) Citizens Advice Brochure ‘Paying for water and sewerage in Scotland’.

9. The Local Authority lodged the following documents:

(a) Breakdown of the Appellant’s council tax, water and sewerage charges for the
periods 2018 to 2023;
(b) Citizens Advice Scotland Information on council tax benefits and water and
sewerage charges;
(c) The Appellant’s Council Tax Notices for 2018/2019, 2019/2020, 2020/2021,
2021/2022 and 2022/2023;
(d) Council Tax Reduction Decision Notices for the Appellant dated 7 December
2018, 9 March 2019, 13 March 2020, 12 March 2021;
(e) Copy of Appeal dated 29 November 2022;
(f) Breakdown of water and wastewater charges for 2021/2022 and 2022/2023;
and
(g) Copy of Scottish Government publication ‘Water services – charging
principles: 2021 to 2027’.

10. In addition both parties had lodged written submissions.

The hearing on 20 May 2024

11. The hearing was held by means of WebEx video conference and started at 11.30
a.m.

12. The appellant was personally present and the respondent was represented by Mrs
Joanna Kane, an Appeals and Liaison Officer with Renfrewshire Council.

13. The tribunal’s clerk asked the parties some initial questions relating to their location
and whether anyone was assisting or supporting them.

14. The legal member then took over the conduct of the hearing, introduced himself and
initially explained the overriding objective to the appellant and the respondent’s
representative

15. The tribunal then noted that parties agreed that the appellant was the tenant of the
property. His landlord was Sanctuary Scotland, a housing association. He had been
a tenant since November 2018 and was still a tenant of the property. It was agreed
that he was the person liable to pay council tax for the property. It was agreed that
he received the single person discount in respect of council tax.

16. The tribunal member also briefly indicated that he was aware of the previous history
of the case involving an earlier tribunal decision which had been quashed by the
Upper Tribunal

17. The tribunal member asked the appellant to set out his position

18. The appellant indicated that he was entirely exempt from council tax. The tribunal
member suggested to the appellant that he was not exempt from council tax but, that
in addition to his discount, he was entitled to certain benefits which covered with his
liability for council tax and that he would not have any payments to make to the
respondent in respect of council tax. The appellant did not seem to accept this
position

19. The tribunal tried to clarify with the appellant whether he understood that the charges
for council tax and the charges for water and sewerage were entirely separate and
asked the appellant to explain why he believed he was entitled to a double discount
on the water and sewage charges.

20. In his written submission he had referred to Water and Sewerage Charges
(Exemption and Reduction) (Scotland) Regulations 2006 (“the 2006 Regulations “)
and in particular regulation 4 of those regulations

21. The relevant provisions of the 2006 Regulations are as follows…

(a) Reduction of Charges: dwellings
(b) 3.  Where–
(c) (a)a person is, under a charges scheme, liable in a relevant year to pay water
charges or sewerage charges, or both;
(d) (b)those charges are payable to a local authority by virtue of the Water
Services Charges (Billing and Collection) (Scotland) Order 2006(6); and
(e) (c)those charges are payable in respect of a dwelling other than a dwelling to
which the 2005 Regulations apply,
(f) the amount payable in respect of those charges shall be subject to the
percentage discount specified in regulation 4 or, as the case may be,
calculated in accordance with regulation 5.
(g) 4.  Where any council tax payable for the dwelling is for any period during a
relevant year subject to a percentage discount under section 79 of the 1992
Act (discounts), then the amount payable in respect of water charges or
sewerage charges, or both, shall during such a period be subject to the same
percentage discount as applies under that section.

22. The appellant quickly became agitated and angry. He did not appear to like being
questioned. He claimed that attempts were being made to charge him twice in respect
of water and sewerage charges. The tribunal member explained that the tribunal was
not responsible for sending him any notices regarding charges nor did the tribunal
issue the charges but was here to deal with his appeal.

23. The appellant then abruptly ended his involvement in the video conference call by
saying “cheerio, I don’t like you” (presumably aimed at the legal member of the
tribunal) and left the video conference call.

24. The hearing had at that point lasted less than ten minutes.

25. The tribunal member then briefly heard from the respondent’s representative who
indicated their position remained as stated in their written representations and
documents  and that she was content for the tribunal member to consider the entirety
of the written representations and supporting documentation  from both parties and
to make a decision on the appeal

26. The tribunal waited for a short period of time from the appellant leaving the
conference call before ending the hearing to see whether he re-joined the call. He
made no attempt to do so

27. The tribunal thereafter concluded the hearing and indicated to the respondent’s
representative that a written decision would be issued

Findings in fact

28. The appellant is the tenant of the property and has resided there since November
2018

29. The appellant is the person liable for  council tax in respect of the property in terms
of the 1992 Act and as such as also liable for the water and sewerage charges in
respect of the property in terms of the 2002 Act

30. The appellant lives alone at the property and has done since taking occupation

31. The appellant is entitled to the appropriate discount in respect of both council tax and
water and sewerage charges on the basis that he is a single person occupying the
property

32. The appellant has received council tax notices from the respondent setting out his
liability for  each of the financial years from November 2018 onwards

33. The council tax notices sent to the appellant have properly and correctly identified
that he is entitled to the single person discount in respect of council tax under the
1992 Act and also identified the appropriate level of discount available to him in
respect of  water and sewerage charges in terms of the relevant legislative provisions

Discussion and reasons for decision

34. In essence the appeal by Mr Mitchell is one where he claims that the respondent has
not given him the benefit of appropriate discounts and exemptions in respect of the
water and sewerage charges for a number of financial years from November 2018 up
to and including the financial year ending 31 March 2023.

35. He claims he is entitled to 50% discount on the water and sewerage charges  in
respect of each of  the financial years 2018/19, 2019/20 and 2020/21 and to a 60%
discount in respect of each financial year from April 2021 onwards, namely the
financial years 2021/22 and 2022/23

36. The appellant’s belief in respect of the financial  years up to and including the year
March 2021  is based upon his interpretation of the Water and Sewerage Charges
(Exemption and Reduction) (Scotland) Regulations 2006.

37. In respect of the financial years from April 2021 onwards it is based on his
interpretation of the Water Charges Reduction Scheme (“WCRS”) which is contained
within a ministerial statement of policy published on 7 December 2020 made by the
Scottish Ministers under the powers given to them in terms of section 29D of the
2002 Act.

38. Mr Mitchell believes that the discount contained in the 2006 Regulations and the
maximum discount contained in the WCRS should be added to the discount to which
he is entitled in respect of council tax as set out in section 79 of the 1992 Act.

39. Section 79 of the 1992 Act provides that a council tax discount will be given to any
chargeable dwelling where there is there is only one resident of the dwelling (“the
single person discount”). That discount is stated to be 25% of the council tax liability

40. Mr Mitchell believes that the single person discount in section 79 of the 1992 Act also
should be applied to his liability for water and sewerage charges before any of the
discounts set out in the 2006 Regulations or the WRCS are then applied. Effectively
he believes that in respect of water and sewerage charge, he is entitled to a double
discount.

41. The respondent does not accept Mr Mitchell’s position. They have set out their
position in their written submission. Their position is that the discounts for council tax
and water and sewerage charges are entirely separate and do not fall to be added
together. No person is entitled to such a double discount. In respect of water and
sewerage charges, the maximum discount available for financial years prior to April
2021 was 25%. The maximum amount of discount available since April 2001 is 35%
in accordance with WCRS.

42. The tribunal has carefully considered the whole of the written submissions and
documents lodged by both parties. It has also taken into account the brief oral
submissions made at the hearing.

43. The tribunal does not agree with Mr. Mitchell’s interpretation of these legislative
provisions. His belief that he is entitled to a double discount is entirely misconceived.

44. Council tax and water and sewerage charges are two entirely separate tax regimes.

45. Council tax is governed by the 1992 Act. Water and sewerage charges are governed
by the 2002 Act. They are two entirely different charges. They may appear each year
on the same notice sent to council tax payers by their local authority but they are
entirely separate legal charges. Water and sewerage charges are not part of the
council tax and are not levied in terms of the 1992 Act. The single person discount
set out in the 1992 Act does not directly extend to water and sewerage charges...

46. The 2006 Regulations indicate that where a person is effectively entitled to the single
person discount in respect of council tax then that person is entitled to the same level
of discount in respect of water and sewerage charges.

47. The interpretation of the 2006 Regulations proposed by Mr Mitchell, that this is a
second and additional 25% reduction in respect of water and sewerage charges, is

one which cannot be supported by a proper reading of the 2006 Regulations and the
1992 Act.  The discount in the 2006 Regulations applies only to water and sewerage
charges and is intended to mirror the single person discount created in the 1992 Act
relating to council tax. It does not create a second or double discount entitlement.
The 2006 Regulations would appear to have been introduced to be complementary
to the single person discount available for council tax by creating a similar discount
for water and sewerage charges.

48. In respect of the water and sewerage charges, he is entitled to a 25% discount for
each of the financial years up to and including the financial year ending in March
2021.  He is not entitled to a double discount on the water and sewerage charges

49. Similarly in respect of the years from April 2021 onwards the Scottish government
have introduced a new system, the WCRS, which allows a discount to certain persons
in respect of the water and sewerage charges

50. In the new system from April 2021 the maximum discount on water and service
charges is clearly stated to be 35%. Again, this is not a second discount to be added
to the single person discount in respect of council tax.

51. It is clear from all the literature published that the maximum discount available in
respect of water and sewage charges under WCRS is currently 35% and has been
since April 2021. This maximum level is clearly stated in the policy document itself. It
is also clearly stated as a maximum in the literature from Citizens Advice Scotland
which has been lodged by both parties as part of the documentation placed before
the tribunal.

52. The tribunal is aware that the initial decision of the First-tier tribunal was quashed by
the Upper Tribunal because it failed to give adequate reasons for the decision
reached. It is regrettable that Mr Mitchell withdrew abruptly from the hearing of 20
May as it meant that the tribunal member was not able to have any proper discussion
with him with regard to the interpretation of the legislation and to discuss with him the
whole background to the legislation which is not set out in his written representations

53. The tribunal notes that in the Upper Tribunal in its decision emphasised that it did not
find that the respondent’s initial decision with regard to the level of discount and
reductions to be applied to the appellant’s water and sewerage charges was wrong
or mistaken. The Upper Tribunal noted that the correct decision may have been made
by both the responded and initial First-tier tribunal. The decision was only overturned
because the reasons provided were inadequate and did not comply with the duty on
the trial to provide a reasoned decision.

54. It is hoped that this decision explains to the appellant in a clear and transparent
manner the basis of the refusal of his appeal.

55. Quite simply put the appellant’s interpretation of the provisions that he believes
support his view that he is entitled to double discount are misconceived

56. The tribunal’s view is that the only possible interpretation of the legislation is that the
discounts introduced in respect of water and sewerage charges are a single separate
discount and are not to be aggregated with the discount available in respect of council
tax.

57. As indicated previously, council tax is separate and distinct from water and sewerage
charges. They have separate initiating legislation and are subject to separate and
distinct regimes in respect of discounts and exemptions. The appellant has received
the discounts to which he is entitled in respect of each and every financial year
involved in this appeal.

58. The appeal is refused and dismissed

Right of Appeal

In terms of Section 46 of the Tribunal (Scotland) Act 2014, a party aggrieved by the
decision of the Tribunal may appeal to the Upper Tribunal for Scotland on a point of
law only. Before an appeal can be made to the Upper Tribunal, the party must first
seek permission to appeal from the First-tier Tribunal. That party must seek
permission to appeal within 30 days of the date the decision was sent to them.

Legal Member

title: FTS/LTC/CT/23/00020: L V Properties LTD v City of Edinburgh Council
text:
Decision of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) under
Section 17 of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland Local Taxation Chamber Rules of
Procedure 2022 (‘The Procedure Rules) and section 81 of the Local Government Finance
Act 1992 in relation to a Council Tax Finance/ Non List appeal against a decision of a
Local Authority.

Chamber Ref:  FTS/LTC/CT/23/00020

Re:
47 Lorne Street, Edinburgh, EH6 8QJ

(“the Property”)

Parties:

L V Properties LTD, 6 Dalhousie Crescent, Dalkeith, Midlothian, EH22 3DP

(“the Appellant”)

City of Edinburgh Council, Income and Benefits Division, PO Box 12331, Edinburgh,
EH7 9DN

(“the Local Authority”)

The First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) (“the Tribunal”)

Tribunal Member:   Andrew McLaughlin

(Legal Member)

Background

The Appellant appeals the decision of the Local Authority to find the Appellant liable for
council tax in respect of the Property for the period of 7 May 2021 until 13 September 2021;

Documents lodged with the Tribunal

The Tribunal had before it emails exchanged between the Appellant and the Local
Authority and submissions with legislation lodged by the Local Authority.

Hearing

This appeal called for a video call hearing at 10 am on 6 July 2023. The Appellant was
represented by Mr Volante who was the named contact of the Appellant. There was no

2
appearance by the Local Authority however they had submitted written representations
and explained in advance that they did not intend to appear and were content to rest on
those representations. Mr Volante did not have any preliminary matters to raise and had
received the submissions produced by the local authority.

Having considered the documentation before it and having heard from Mr Volante, the
Tribunal made the following findings in fact, and findings in fact and law.

Findings in Fact

I.
The last occupier of the Property died on 07/08/14;
II.
The Appellant purchased the Property on 07/05/21;
III.
The Property was purchased in a derelict state and had been unoccupied for
several years;
IV.
The Property was removed from the domestic Council Tax list on 13/09/21;
V.
The Appellant is liable for Council Tax for the period 07/05/21 to 13/09/21 on the
basis that they are the owner of an unoccupied dwelling in the Council Tax
valuation list;
Findings in Fact and Law
I.
The Property was listed as a band B dwelling during the period 01/04/97 to
13/09/21;
II.
The Local Government Finance Act 1992 defines a resident as ‘an individual who
has attained the age of 18 years old and has his sole or main residence in the
dwelling;
III.
The previous occupant of the Property died on 07/08/14;
IV.
The Local Government Finance Act 1975 sets out that where there is no resident
in the dwelling the owner of the dwelling is liable for Council Tax;
V.
A dwelling can be exempt from Council Tax if it meets the conditions of the
Empty Dwelling Exemption criteria contains within Schedule 1 of the Council
Tax (Exempt Dwellings) (Scotland) Order 1997, as amended by the Council Tax
(Exempt Dwelling) Scotland) Amendment Order 2012 with effect from 01/04/13;
VI.
The exemption criteria states that a dwelling must be unoccupied and
unfurnished and less than six months have lapsed since the end of the last period
of three months or more throughout which it was continuously occupied;
VII.
The Council Tax Exempt Dwellings Scotland Order 1997 as amended by The
Council Tax (Exempt Dwellings) (Scotland) Amendment (No2) Order 1999 Sets
the criteria that an unoccupied dwelling is exempt from Council Tax if it is
undergoing or undergone structural alteration or major repair work to make it
habitable. The exemption is limited to twelve months from then the dwelling was

3
last occupied, or up to six months after the works has been substantially
completed.
VIII.
Schedule 1 (8) of The Council Tax Exempt Dwellings Scotland Order 1997
allows an exemption to be awarded where a property is awaiting demolition.
However, the legislation set the condition that the dwelling must be owned by a
local authority or Scottish Homes. Scottish Homes was replaced by Scottish
Communities in 2001. They were responsible for providing affordable housing
and environmental protections. That organisation was in turn replaced by the
Scottish Housing Regulator in 2011;
Note:-

I.
The substance of the appeal is that the Local Authority’s decision is unfair. The
Local Authority correctly note that it is not in the jurisdiction of the Local
Authority or the Tribunal to vary legislation set by the Scottish Government
based on an individual’s assessment of the fairness of that legislation;
II.
The test that must be applied is whether the appellant legally qualifies for an
exemption during the period 07/05/21 to 13/09/21;
III.
The wording of the legislation for the exemptions is precise and for the purposes
of the appeal, the Local Authority need only to demonstrate that the law has been
followed;
IV.
Exemptions fall into two categories that are either exemption based on the
circumstances of the dwelling, or exemptions based on the circumstances of the
liable party. The eligibility to these exemptions are time limited for a maximum
of six months (for an empty dwelling) and twelve months (for a dwelling under
repair) from the date that the dwelling was last occupied. The change of
ownership does not have any effect on the last occupation date;
V.
The Local Authority has refused to award the empty dwelling exemption on the
ground that more than six months had passed since the end of the last period of
three months or more throughout which it was continuously occupied;
VI.
The Local Authority has refused the dwelling under repair exemption on the
ground that that more than six months had passed since the end of the last
period of three months or more throughout which it was continuously occupied;
VII.
The Local Authority has refused to award a dwelling awaiting demolition
exemption because the appellant is not a private owner and does not meet the
criteria prescribed in legislation.

Decision
Having made the above findings and having adjourned to consider its decision, the
Tribunal therefore refuses the appeal.

4

6. Right of Appeal

In terms of Section 46 of the Tribunal (Scotland) Act 2014, a party aggrieved by the
decision of the Tribunal may appeal to the Upper Tribunal for Scotland on a point of
law only. Before an appeal can be made to the Upper Tribunal, the party must first seek
permission to appeal from the First-tier Tribunal. That party must seek permission to
appeal within 30 days of the date the decision was sent to them.
