title: FTS/LTC/CT/23/00021: Shona MacDonald v City of Edinburgh Council
text:
REGULATION ‐ SENSITIVE
Decision of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) under
Section 17 of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland Local Taxation Chamber Rules
of Procedure 2022 (‘The Procedure Rules) and section 81 of the Local
Government Finance Act 1992 in relation to an Council Tax Finance/ Non List
appeal against a decision of a Local Authority.

Chamber Ref:  FTS/LTC/CT/23/00021

Re:

24/5 Bailie Terrace, Edinburgh, EH15 3BU (“the Property”)

Parties:

Shona MacDonald  (“the Appellant”)

City of Edinburgh Council (“the Local Authority”)

The First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) (“the Tribunal”)

Tribunal Member:    Fiona Watson
(Legal Member)

Background

1. The Appellant appeals the decision of the Local Authority in calculating the
council tax liability pertaining to the Property from 30 June 2021 to date.
Reference is made to s81(1)b) of the Local Government Finance Act 1992 (“the
1992 Act”) as set out below:

81 Appeal to the First-tier Tribunal.
(1)A person may appeal to the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland if he is aggrieved
by—
(a)any decision of a local authority that a dwelling is a chargeable dwelling, or
that he is liable to pay council tax in respect of such a dwelling; or
(b)any calculation made by a local authority of an amount which he is liable to
pay to the authority in respect of council tax,
and the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland shall make such decision as they think
just.

2. The Appellant has notified the Local Authority in writing, on 19 December 2022,
that they wish to challenge the decision of the Local Authority. Thereafter, the

REGULATION ‐ SENSITIVE
Appellant has notified the Local Authority that they intend to appeal the decision
of the Local Authority, as required under s81(4) of the said 1992 Act.

Hearing

3. This case called for a Hearing on 18 August 2023, which Hearing took place in-
person.

4. The Appellant represented herself. The Local Authority had lodged written
submissions with the Tribunal in advance of the Hearing and had confirmed
that they did not intend to appear nor be represented at the Hearing.

Documents lodged with the Tribunal.

5. Documents lodged with the Tribunal by the Appellant were:

(i)
Letter from Appellant together with photographs, dated 18 April 2023;
(ii)
Letter from Appellant to Local Authority dated 6 February 2023
(iii)
Email correspondence between the Appellant and the Local Authority
dated 4 March 2023 to 29 March 2023
(iv)
Written submissions from Local Authority together with attachments,
dated 25 April 2023.

Decision

6. The First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) refuses the
appeal.

Findings in Fact.

7. The Tribunal made the following findings in fact:

(i)
The Appellant is the owner of the Property;
(ii)
The Property was rented out to a tenant until 30 June 2021;
(iii)
The Property was substantially damaged by fire on 11 July 2021 and
remains under repair.
(iv)
The Appellant is the liable party for payment of council tax for the period 11
July 2023 to date.

Reasons for Decision

8. The Appellant stated that she owns the Property which had been rented to a
tenant until 30 June 2021, at which point the tenant vacated.  On 11 July 2021,

REGULATION ‐ SENSITIVE
the Property was substantially damaged by fire, along with the other properties
in the building of which it forms part. The Property remains under repair.

9. The Appellant stated that the Property is uninhabitable. It was stated that the
Local Authority had offered to the Appellant and the other owners in the building
that they would carry out the necessary works to make the building safe, to
allow each owner to then carry out their own internal property works. The
Appellant stated that she has been liaising with her insurer and contractor to
gain access to the Property to effect the necessary repairs but that the Local
Authority has restricted access. The Appellant stated that two of the properties
in the stair are owned by the Local Authority and both have been made safe
and both have been refurbished both internally and externally. The remaining
six properties in the stair are privately owned and the Local Authority has
prevented the Appellant and the other owners from carrying out work to their
properties in a timeous manner. It was stated that the Local Authority failed to
carry out sufficient works for a period of 14 months from the date of the fire. The
Appellant stated that whilst she acknowledged that the Local Authority had
applied certain exemptions to the council tax to date, they have advised her
that she will only be awarded a 10% discount on the council tax from 1 August
2023 whilst the Property remains unoccupied and further, from 1 February
2024, a 100% additional charge will be levied should the Property continue to
remain unoccupied. The Appellant submitted that this was not fair, and that she
did not consider that she should have to pay any council tax for so long as the
Property remained uninhabitable. The Appellant submitted that she could not
afford to pay council tax for the both the property she resides in, as well as the
Property under repair. The Appellant was unable to direct the Tribunal to any
particular exemption or discount that she considered should have been applied,
or could be applied, by the Local Authority. Ther Appellant submitted that she
simply considered that this was an unfair situation as she could not rent the
Property out in its current state. She considered that the delay in repairs being
effected was due to inaction on the part of the Local Authority and not due to
any fault on her part.

10. The Tribunal noted from the Local Authority’s written submissions that the Local
Authority determined that the Appellant’s liability for payment of council tax for
the Property commenced on 30 June 2021, in her capacity as owner of the
Property following the departure of her tenant. An empty dwelling exemption
had been applied for the period 30 June 2021 to 10 July 2021. A dwelling under
repair exemption was thereafter applied for the period 11 July 2021 (being the
date of the fire) to 29 June 2022. The Local Authority thereafter made a decision
to apply a further such exemption for 12 months from 30 June 2021 to 31 July
2023. The Local Authority submitted that no further exemptions are available.

11. Whilst the Tribunal had some sympathy with the Appellant and noted that these
must be difficult circumstances for her, the Tribunal was satisfied that the Local
Authority was entitled to hold the Appellant liable for payment of council tax as
the owner of the Property from the period of 30 June 2021, in terms of the
provisions of s75 of the Local Government Finance Act 1992.

REGULATION ‐ SENSITIVE
12.  The Tribunal was satisfied that in terms of The Council Tax Exempt Dwellings
Scotland Order 1997 as amended, an exemption can be applied to a Property
which is an unoccupied dwelling where it is undergoing structural alteration of
major repair work to make it habitable, and that such an exemption is limited to
twelve months from when the dwelling was last occupied or up to six months
after the works have been substantially completed.

13. The Tribunal noted that the substance of the Appellant’s appeal was that she
considered that the said exemption should be extended further until such time
as the Property was repaired and habitable again to be re-let.  The Tribunal
was not persuaded by the Appellant that there was any basis in law for such a
proposition and such an extension was not provided for in the said 1997 Order.

14. It was noted that the Appellant made certain submissions regarding the delays
in being able to complete the repair works being due to inaction and/or delays
on the part of the Local Authority.  Such issues are outwith the jurisdiction of
the Tribunal and accordingly the Tribunal can make no determination in that
regard.

15. Against that background, the Tribunal refuses the appeal.

Right of Appeal

In terms of Section 46 of the Tribunal (Scotland) Act 2014, a party aggrieved by
the decision of the Tribunal may appeal to the Upper Tribunal for Scotland on a
point of law only. Before an appeal can be made to the Upper Tribunal, the party
must first seek permission to appeal from the First-tier Tribunal. That party must
seek permission to appeal within 30 days of the date the decision was sent to
them.

title: FTS/LTC/CT/23/00023: Fraser Meighan v Heather Meighan (“the Appellant’s Representative”) City of Edinburgh Council
text:
Decision of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) under
Section 17 of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland Local Taxation Chamber Rules
of Procedure 2022 (‘The Procedure Rules) and section 81 of the Local
Government Finance Act 1992 in relation to an Council Tax Finance/ Non List
appeal against a decision of a Local Authority.

Chamber Ref:  FTS/LTC/CT/23/00023

Re: 245(2F2) Dalkeith Road, Edinburgh, EH16 5JS (“the Property”)

Parties:

Fraser Meighan (“the Appellant”)

Heather Meighan (“the Appellant’s Representative”)

City of Edinburgh Council (“the Local Authority”)

The First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) (“the Tribunal”)

Tribunal Member:    Fiona Watson (Legal Member)

Background

1. The Appellant appeals the decision of the Local Authority not to apply a student
disregard when calculating the council tax liability pertaining to the Property
during the period 1 June 2022 to 4 September 2022. Reference is made to
s81(1)b) of the Local Government Finance Act 1992 (“the 1992 Act”) as set out
below:

81 Appeal to the First-tier Tribunal.
(1)A person may appeal to the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland if he is aggrieved
by—
(a)any decision of a local authority that a dwelling is a chargeable dwelling, or
that he is liable to pay council tax in respect of such a dwelling; or
(b)any calculation made by a local authority of an amount which he is liable to
pay to the authority in respect of council tax,

and the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland shall make such decision as they think
just.
2. The Appellant has notified the Local Authority in writing, on 6 November 2022,
that they wish to challenge the decision of the Local Authority. Thereafter, on
29 January 2023, the Appellant has notified the Local Authority that they intend
to appeal the decision of the Local Authority, as required under s81(4) of the
said 1992 Act.

3. The Appellant was the occupier of the Property between the period 17 June
2021 and 4 September 2022. It is not known from the papers whether the
Appellant continues to reside in the Property, but this is not relevant for the
purposes of determining this appeal.

4. The Appellant was a full-time undergraduate student at the University of
Edinburgh between 17 June 2021 and 31 May 2022. The Local Authority
applied a student exemption from paying council tax for that period. The Local
Authority deemed the date 31 May 2022 to be the default date of the end of the
period of the Appellant’s undergraduate study. This does not appear to be in
dispute.

5. The Appellant thereafter commenced a programme of postgraduate study at
the University of Strathclyde, which commenced 5 September 2022.

6. The Local Authority has decided that the Appellant is not entitled to a student
disregard during the period 1 June 2022 to 4 September 2022, reflecting the
period between the end of the Appellant’s undergraduate course of education
and the commencement of the Appellant’s postgraduate course of education.
The Local Authority has awarded the Appellant a 25% single person discount
for that period.

7. The Local Authority has awarded a student exemption thereafter for the period
5 September 2022 to 25 September 2022. It is not known from the papers the
relevance of the date 25th September 2022 but this is not required for the
purposes of determining this appeal.

8. The Appellant seeks to challenge the decision of the Local Authority not to
award a student disregard for the period 1 June 2022 to 4 September 2022.
The Appellant’s representative (being his mother) states as follows:

“My son is studying to become a Scottish lawyer. There are two constituent
parts to professional legal study in Scotland comprising: undergraduate LLB
which is a 4-year course. a postgraduate diploma in law course which takes a
year. Both courses are mandatory... Whilst there was a break in courses
between the LLB and the postgraduate diploma, the foundation of your claim
that Fraser is liable for council tax payment during this break, there is no choice
to this pattern of study for law students. Consequently, Fraser has been a
committed law student throughout five years of study, as is required of him, and
should not be liable for council tax payments during the summer months. I

would compare this to other university degrees that last five years and whereby
council tax exemption applies throughout.”

9. Further it is noted in the papers that in what appears to be an online form
submitted to the Local Authority dated 29 January 2023, the Appellant’s
representative states “the regulations are discriminatory and need to be
updated. They take no account of different undergraduate degrees and
durations and impose charges on some students but not others.”

Documents lodged with the Tribunal.

10. Documents lodged with the Tribunal were:

(i)
Appellant’s Higher Education Achievement Report dated 9 January 2022
(ii)
Email exchange between Local Authority and Appellant’s representative
dated 3 and 6 November 2022
(iii)
Response from Local Authority to Applicant dated 18 January 2023
(iv)
Notice from Appellant to Local Authority dated 29 January 2023
(v)
Email from Local Authority to Tribunal dated 27 April 2023
(vi)
Written Submission by Local Authority to Tribunal dated 26 May 2023
(vii)
Form entitled “Request council tax certificate” (undated)
(viii)
Copy of The Council Tax (Discounts) (Scotland) Consolidation and
Amendment Order 2003
(ix)
Copy of the Council Tax (Discounts) (Scotland) Amendment Order 2011

Hearing

11. The parties agreed that no hearing was required and that the appeal could be
determined by the Tribunal on the basis of the written submissions of the
parties.

Decision

12. The First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) refuses the
appeal.

Findings in Fact.

13. The Tribunal made the following findings in fact:

(i)
The Appellant was a full-time undergraduate student with the University
of Edinburgh between 17 June 2021 and 31 May 2022;
(ii)
The Appellant was a full-time postgraduate student with the University
of Strathclyde commencing 5 September 2022;
(iii)
The Appellant was not enrolled in a programme of study with an
educational establishment during the period 1 June 2022 and 4
September 2022;
(iv)
The Appellant had no entitlement to a student disregard for council tax
for the period 1 June 2022 and 4 September 2022.

Reasons for Decision

14. Regulation 6 of The Council Tax (Discounts) (Scotland) Consolidation and
Amendment Order 2003, as amended, sets out the requirements to be met for
a student disregard, as follows:
6. - (1) For the purposes of paragraph 4 of Schedule 1 to the Act, “student”
means a person who, on a particular day, is not a student nurse (in terms of
article 7) and is–
(a)registered with the Central Bureau for Educational Visits and Exchanges as
a foreign language assistant, provided that the day falls within the period of the
person’s appointment as such an assistant at a school or other educational
institution in Great Britain;
(b)aged under 20 and undertaking with a single educational establishment
(otherwise than in consequence of an office or employment held by the
person)–
(i)a qualifying course of education in respect of which the relevant number of
hours per week exceeds 12; or
(ii)two or more qualifying courses of education in respect of which the aggregate
of the relevant number of hours per week for all those courses exceeds 12; or
(c)undertaking a course of education–
(i)which is specified in Schedule 2 to this Order;
(ii)which is provided by an institution specified in Schedule 3 to this Order;
(iii)which requires the attendance of persons undertaking it for a period of at
least 24 weeks within each academic year of the institution providing it; and
(iv)in respect of which, in the opinion of the institution, a person would ordinarily
require to undertake periods of study or tuition (including any periods of
industrial, professional or commercial experience associated with the course
which the person requires to undertake to complete the course) which amount,
in the aggregate, to an average of at least 21 hours a week during the period
mentioned in head (iii) above.
(2) A person is to be regarded for the purposes of paragraph (1)(b) as
undertaking a qualifying course of education on a particular day if–
(a)the day falls within the relevant period for that course; and
(b)the person is not on that day an apprentice or a youth training trainee (in
terms of article 5 or 8).

(3) A person is to be regarded for the purposes of paragraph (1)(c) as
undertaking a course of education on a particular day if–
(a)on the day the person is enrolled with the institution providing the course for
the purpose of attending that course; and
(b)the day falls within the period beginning with the day on which the person
begins the course and ending with the day on which the person ceases to
undertake it, and for these purposes a person is to be regarded as ceasing to
undertake a course of education if the person has completed it, abandoned it
or is no longer permitted by the institution to attend it.

15. The Appellant has provided no evidence to show that he has undertaken a
qualifying course of education for the period 1 June 2022 and 4 September
2022, and which would entitle him to a student disregard for that period, as is
required in terms of Regulation 6. By the Appellant’s own admission, he was
not enrolled in a programme of study with an educational establishment during
that period. The Appellant has undertaken two separate courses of further
education. The Appellant completed his undergraduate degree by 31 May 2022
and there is no evidence before the tribunal that the appellant was enrolled as
a student an undertaking a qualifying course of education at any educational
establishment until he commenced his postgraduate course of education with
the University of Strathclyde on 5 September 2022.

16. The Tribunal is not persuaded by the position put forward by the Appellant that
his situation is comparable to other university degrees that last five years. The
appellant
has
undertaken
two
separate
educational
courses
(one
undergraduate course lasting four years, and thereafter one postgraduate
course) each with a separate educational establishment. Whilst it is accepted
by the Tribunal that the Appellant requires to undertake both of these courses
in order to commence a traineeship as a Scottish solicitor, the Tribunal does
not consider that this puts the Appellant at any greater disadvantage than any
other student undertaking two separate university courses in close succession,
such as an undergraduate university course followed by a postgraduate
Masters degree. Where a student undertakes a 5-year undergraduate degree,
they are a student under that particular, and singular, course of education for
that five-year period. The situations are not comparable.

17. The Tribunal is satisfied that the Local Authority has not erred in law in coming
to the decision reached, being not to award a student exemption for the period
1 June 2022 to 4 September 2022, and on that basis the appeal is refused.

Right of Appeal

In terms of Section 46 of the Tribunal (Scotland) Act 2014, a party aggrieved by
the decision of the Tribunal may appeal to the Upper Tribunal for Scotland on a
point of law only. Before an appeal can be made to the Upper Tribunal, the party
must first seek permission to appeal from the First-tier Tribunal. That party must
seek permission to appeal within 30 days of the date the decision was sent to
them.

title: FTS/LTC/CT/23/00024: Dr Gillian Houston v City of Edinburgh Council
text:
Decision of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) under
Section 17 of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland Local Taxation Chamber Rules of
Procedure 2022 (‘The Procedure Rules) and section 81 of the Local Government Finance
Act 1992 in relation to a Council Tax Finance/ Non List appeal against a decision of a
Local Authority.

Chamber Ref:  FTS/LTC/CT/23/00024

Re:  Milton Cottage, Dalmeny, West Lothian, EH30 9SR

(“the Property”)

Parties:
Dr Gillian Houston, Milton Cottage, Dalmeny, West Lothian, EH30 9SR

(“the Appellant”)

City of Edinburgh Council, Income and Benefit Division, PO Box 12331, Edinburgh,
EH7 9DN

(“the Local Authority”)

The First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) (“the Tribunal”)

Tribunal Member:  Andrew McLaughlin

(Legal Member)

Background

The Appellant appeals the decision of the Local Authority to refuse a further dwelling
under repair exemption under the Council Tax (Exempt Dwellings) (Scotland) Order 1997
as amended by the Council Tax (Exempt Dwellings) (Scotland) Amendment (No.2) Order
1999

Documents lodged with the Tribunal

The Tribunal had before it emails exchanged between the parties, a document setting
out the reasons for the appeal together with written representations from the Local
Authority setting out their position.

2

Hearing

This case called for a video call hearing at 2pm on 6 July 2023. The Appellant was
personally present. There was no appearance by or on behalf of the Respondent on the
basis that they had indicated that they did not intend to appear and wished to rely on
their written representations.

Dr Houston confirmed that she had no preliminary matters to raise and had received all
the relevant documentation.

Having considered all the documentation before the Tribunal and having heard from Dr
Houston, the Tribunal made the following findings in fact.

Findings in Fact

I.
The Appellant is the proprietor of the Property along with her partner, Mr Alan Conner;
II.
The Appellant purchased the Property in 2016;
III.
On 6 August 2021, the Property was struck by lightning and badly damaged;
IV.
The Appellant has not been able to live in the Property since then which is still currently
being repaired;
V.
The Appellant received a dwelling under repair exemption for the period 6 August 2021 to
5 August 2022. This was as per the terms of the Council Tax (Exempt Dwellings)
(Scotland) order 1997 as amended by the Council Tax (Exempt Dwellings) (Scotland)
Amendment (No.2) Order 1999;
VI.
The last date of occupation of the Property was 6 August 2021;
VII.
The Local Authority informed the Appellant that the dwelling under repair exemption had
expired and now the Appellant was liable for council tax;
VIII.
The Appellant does not live in the Property and repairs remain ongoing;
IX.
There is currently no legal prohibition that prevents entry to the Property even for the
purpose of construction and repair. Workers are currently continuing to restore the
Property.

Reasons for decision

I.
The Appeal is based on the Appellant’s perception that it is unfair that a further
dwelling under repair exemption cannot be granted over and above the original
exemption.
II.
It is hard not to have a great deal of sympathy to the Appellant who finds herself
liable for council tax on the Property despite not being able to live in it. However,
the terms of the Council Tax (Exempt Dwellings) (Scotland) Order 1997 as
amended by the Council Tax (Exempt Dwellings) (Scotland) Amendment (No.2)

3
Order 1999 are such that any exemption is limited to twelve months from the last
day of occupation.
III.
The Tribunal notes the Appellant’s position that Covid caused delays to works
being progressed. However no legislative discretion exists that might allow the
Tribunal the ability to competently grant this Appeal.
IV.
The terms of the legislation are such that this appeal must be refused.
V.
The Tribunal considered whether an exemption could be granted on account of
occupation of the Property being prohibited by law. The Tribunal considered the
decision of the Inner House of the Court of Session in the case of City of Edinburgh
Council vs the Lothian Valuation Appeal Committee (2014 CSIH 32 XA16/13).
VI.
In that case it was held that such an exemption could only apply if there was a
legal notice that prevents entry to the Property even for the purpose of
construction/repair. There is no such prohibition in this case.

Decision

Having made the above findings, the Tribunal refuses the appeal.

Right of Appeal

In terms of Section 46 of the Tribunal (Scotland) Act 2014, a party aggrieved by the
decision of the Tribunal may appeal to the Upper Tribunal for Scotland on a point of
law only. Before an appeal can be made to the Upper Tribunal, the party must first seek
permission to appeal from the First-tier Tribunal. That party must seek permission to
appeal within 30 days of the date the decision was sent to them.

title: FTS/LTC/CT/23/00027: Elaine Patterson v South Lanarkshire Council
text:
Decision of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) under
Section 17 of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland Local Taxation Chamber Rules
of Procedure 2022 (‘The Procedure Rules) and section 81 of the Local
Government Finance Act 1992 in relation to an Council Tax Finance/ Non List
appeal against a decision of a Local Authority.

Chamber Ref:  FTS/LTC/CT/23/00027

Re: 4 Glenafton View, Hamilton, ML3 8DY (“the Property”)

Parties:

Elaine Patterson, 1 Loanburn Avenue, Penicuik, Midlothian, EH26 8BJ (“the
Appellant”)

South Lanarkshire Council, PO Box 3591, Glasgow, G73 9ED (“the Local
Authority”)

The First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) (“the Tribunal”)

Tribunal Member:    Fiona Watson
(Legal Member)

Background

1. The Appellant appeals the decision of the Local Authority to apply an empty
property surcharge to the Property for the period 4 April 2021 to 30 November
2021. Reference is made to s81(1)b) of the Local Government Finance Act
1992 (“the 1992 Act”) as set out below:

81 Appeal to the First-tier Tribunal.
(1)A person may appeal to the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland if he is aggrieved
by—
(a)any decision of a local authority that a dwelling is a chargeable dwelling, or
that he is liable to pay council tax in respect of such a dwelling; or
(b)any calculation made by a local authority of an amount which he is liable to
pay to the authority in respect of council tax,
and the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland shall make such decision as they think
just.

2. The Appellant has notified the Local Authority in writing, on 10 October 2022,
that they wish to challenge the decision of the Local Authority. Thereafter, on
11 November 2022, the Appellant has notified the Local Authority that they
intend to appeal the decision of the Local Authority, as required under s81(4)
of the said 1992 Act.

Hearing

3. This case called for a Hearing on 28 August 2023, which Hearing took place by
Webex video call.

4. The Appellant represented herself. The Local Authority was represented by
Bryan Robertson, Officer of South Lanarkshire Council.

5. The Appellant submitted that the Property was rented out to a tenant who
stopped paying rent in around September 2019. That tenant left the property in
April 2020, leaving the Property in a state of extreme disrepair. It was submitted
that because the Property was empty for more than six months from that date,
the Local Authority now wish to charge the Appellant double council tax.

6. The Appellant submitted that she lives in Midlothian and the property is located
in South Lanarkshire. At the time of the tenant leaving the Property, there were
a lot of COVID restrictions which prohibited travelling between different local
authority areas. The Appellant submitted that the tenant had left a lot of
belongings in the Property. The Appellant submitted that she sought advice as
to her legal position at that stage and was advised that she was not permitted
to do anything as regards the tenant’s belongings for a period of three months.
The Appellant submitted that the Local Authority granted an exemption from
payment of council tax for the period 5 April 2020 to 4 October 2020. The
Appellant submitted that this three-month period in which she was unable to
clear the Property took up half of the time in which the local authority had
granted an exemption.

7. The Appellant submitted that she required to clear the Property and carry out
significant repairs, and had a restricted income during that time. This took her
time to complete and get the Property back into a state that she could re-let.
The Appellant submitted that as the tenant was in receipt of benefits, the
Appellant was not entitled to ongoing landlord insurance cover.

8. The Appellant submitted that the Local Authority’s policy on whether or not they
charge the unoccupied charge sates that this is at their discretion. The
Appellant submitted that the Local Authority have the discretion not to impose
the charge and they have chosen not to do so. The Appellant submitted that it
is the sum of £1263.72 which is in dispute. The Property was empty for a full
year. The Appellant submitted that the Property was in a horrendous condition,
with dirty nappies, rubbish bags, piles of clothes etc. She required to plaster
walls, replace all carpets, worktops, sinks, light fittings etc and the whole
Property required to be repainted. The Appellant submitted that she only has
one property that she lets out. Due to the covid restrictions she was unable to

travel from Midlothian into South Lanarkshire and she did not have sufficient
income to be able to pay people to do the work for her. She required to do the
work herself and had to borrow money from her parents to carry out certain
works.

9. The Local Authority confirmed that their position was as set out in their written
submission. After the initial six-month exemption had been applied, the Local
Authority awarded a 50% discount on the council tax for a further six months.
The Local Authority submitted that in relation to the discretionary aspect of the
empty property surcharge, the legislation gives local authorities some
discretion, and it is for each local authority to make their own policy. The policy
of South Lanarkshire Council is that after 12 months, a surcharge is applied.
The policy does not provide for any discretion for exemptions to be made in
individual circumstances. The Local Authority submitted that whilst they have
sympathy for the situation that the Appellant finds herself in, the Local
Authority’s hands are tied. The unoccupied property exemption cannot be
awarded for more than a six-month period. The Local Authority has discretion
regarding the discount to be applied thereafter, and which discretion they used
to apply a discount at the rate of 50% for a further six-month period. The Local
Authority submitted that after that 12-month period, the legislation gives local
authorities flexibility to determine their own policy, and South Lanarkshire
Council’s policy is that the empty property surcharge is imposed after 12
months of a property being unoccupied and is set at 200%. It was submitted
that the legislation ties the Local Authority’s hands, and the council's own policy
ties the staff’s hands in terms of what they can do for individual owners. It was
submitted that the Local Authority has acted in accordance with the law and in
accordance with the Local Authority’s own policy.

10. The Local Authority submitted that the Appellant gave a date of 5 April 2020 as
the date that the tenancy had ended. The Local Authority accepted that date. It
was submitted that the issue raised by the Appellant as regards the tenant
leaving her belongings in the Property would not change the date of the end of
tenancy and would not change the position that the Property was unoccupied
from that date. As the tenant was not occupying the Property as their sole or
main residence beyond 5 April 2020, the Local Authority cannot hold the tenant
liable for payment of council tax and because the Property was not occupied,
that is a starting point for the non-occupied exemption. It was submitted that
even though there were restraints during the COVID period, there was no
change to the council tax legislation regarding the exemptions that could be
applied during that period, and there was no change to the Local Authority’s
policy. It was submitted that the Local Authority has awarded the maximum
exemption that it is able to award and has followed their own policy thereafter.

11. The Appellant submitted that she thought the 200% surcharge to be very unfair.
It was submitted that the policy was put in place by the Local Authority and that
it is within the Local Authority’s power to change that policy taking into account
individual mitigating circumstances. The Appellant submitted that she found it
very unfair to be charged 200% council tax under the circumstances and
particularly where she was already thousands of pounds out of pocket due to
her former tenant failing to pay rent and causing damage to the Property.

Documents lodged with the Tribunal.

12. Documents lodged with the Tribunal by the Appellant were:

(i)
Local Authority’s written submissions dated 25 April 2023
(ii)
Copy online form dated 25 August 2022 completed by Appellant
(iii)
Copy letter written by Appellant’s mother dated 25 August 2022
(iv)
Emails between Local Authority and Appellant dated 23 September
2022 to 23 November 2022

Decision

13. The First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) refuses the
appeal.

Findings in Fact.

14. The Tribunal made the following findings in fact:

(i)
The Appellant is the owner of the Property;
(ii)
The Appellant is the liable party for payment of council tax for the period 4
April 2020 to 30 November 2021;
(iii)
The Property was unoccupied from 4 April 2020 to 30 November 2021;
(iv)
The Local Authority has applied an exemption from 5 April 2020 to 4 October
2020, followed by a 50% discount from 5 October 2020 to 4 April 2021;
(v)
The Local Authority is entitled to impose a 200% council tax charge from 5
April 2021 to date of re-occupation.

Reasons for Decision

15. The Tribunal was satisfied that the Local Authority was entitled to reach the
decision that it did. The Tribunal has not been persuaded by the Appellant that
the Local Authority has erred in law.

16.  The Tribunal was satisfied that liability for payment of council tax reverted to
the Appellant as owner of the Property on 4 April 2020, following the Property
becoming unoccupied upon the departure of the former tenant.

17. The Local Authority granted an exemption for an initial period of 6 months
covering the period 5 April 2020 to 4 October 2020, being the maximum period
permitted in terms of The Council Tax (Exempt Dwellings) (Scotland) Order
1997 (as amended).  Thereafter a 50% discount was awarded for the period 5
October 2020 to 4 April 2021, being the maximum 6-month period permitted
under the Local Authority’s policy and in terms of The Council Tax (Variation
for Unoccupied Dwellings) (Scotland) Regulations 2013, (as amended).

18. The Appellant takes issue with the application of the empty property surcharge
from 5 April 2021, which effectively imposes 200% council tax, due to the
Property continuing to be unoccupied for more than 12 months.  This surcharge
is applied in terms of the said 2013 Regulations and in terms of the Local
Authority’s own policy. The Appellant has failed to satisfy the Tribunal that the
Local Authority has erred in law in applying said surcharge, which the Tribunal
is satisfied the Local Authority was entitled to do in terms of the said
Regulations. It is admitted by the Appellant that the Property has been
unoccupied for more than 12 months. The Tribunal notes the Appellant’s
position that she was unable to re-let the property earlier due to her own
personal financial constraints and covid restrictions meaning she could not
carry out the works required to the Property within a quicker timescale, and the
Tribunal has some sympathy with the Appellant finding herself in such
circumstances. Whilst this is unfortunate for the Appellant, and more so given
the Appellant did not appear to have adequate insurance cover for such losses,
regardless of the Appellant’s particular circumstances, the Tribunal is not
persuaded that the Local Authority have erred in law in applying such a
surcharge and calculating the council tax as they did.  Accordingly, the appeal
is refused.

Right of Appeal

In terms of Section 46 of the Tribunal (Scotland) Act 2014, a party aggrieved by
the decision of the Tribunal may appeal to the Upper Tribunal for Scotland on a
point of law only. Before an appeal can be made to the Upper Tribunal, the party
must first seek permission to appeal from the First-tier Tribunal. That party must
seek permission to appeal within 30 days of the date the decision was sent to
them.

The hearing

A hearing was assigned for 28 June 2023. The appellant appeared on his own

6.
Both the appellant and Mr Robertson relied on the documents lodged and made
submissions.

Findings in Fact;

7.
The tribunal found the following facts admitted or proved.

8.
The appellant is the heritable proprietor of the dwelling. The dwelling is a flat in
a tenant building of three floors with two flats on each floor. There is an adjoining
tenement also of three floors with two flats on each floor.

9.
As at 3 May 2021 the dwelling had been let and was occupied by tenants.

10.
On 3 May 2021 there was an explosion in a flat in the adjoining the tenement
building. The flats in the both tenements were evacuated on safety grounds.

11.
The dwelling was last occupied on 3 May 2021.

12.
On the advice of the respondent the appellant applied for and was granted a
council tax exemption on the basis that the dwelling was a dwelling under repair
in terms of Schedule 1 para. 2 of The Council Tax (Exempt Dwellings)
(Scotland) Order 1997 (the 1997 Order).

13.
On 12 May 2022 the respondent emailed the appellant advising him that as the
dwelling under repair exemption was limited to a maximum of 12 months under
the 1997 Order, the exemption had ended on 2 May 2022.

14.
From 3 May 2022 the respondent allowed the appellant a 50% discount on the
council tax in accordance with the Council Tax (Variation for Unoccupied
Dwellings) (Scotland) Regulations 2013 (the 2013 Regulations). This discount
is allowable for a maximum of 6 months after the exemption ended.

15.
Apart from a period on one day shortly after 3 May 2021 (when access to the
dwelling was allowed to recover personal effects) and one day shortly before
24 October 2022 (when access to the dwelling was allowed to assess damage)
the respondent prevented the appellant from having access to or being able to
occupy the dwelling from 3 May 2021 to 24 October 2022.

16.
By email dated 21 December 2022 the respondent advised the appellant that
following further information from their Housing Project Manager they were

4

satisfied that occupation of the property was prohibited by law and as such an
exemption was awarded under that category for the period 3 May 2021 to 23
October 2022 (the day before access was permitted). The respondent
thereafter allowed the remainder of the 6 month 50% discount allowable after
a property had been unoccupied for 12 months from 24 October to 2 November
2022.

17.
The respondent applied the increased amount of council tax payable of 100%
in respect of the dwelling, in terms of their policy, from 3 November 2022.

18.
The liability to pay the increased amount of council tax payable of 100%   ended
on 20 February 2023.

Evidence and submissions

The Appellant
19.
The facts of the case were not in dispute. The issue was whether the
respondent was correct to apply an increased amount of council tax as payable,
or what is commonly referred to as the empty property the surcharge.
20.
He had been denied access to the dwelling. The dwelling was one of 6 flats in
a tenement. There was an adjoining tenement. There was an explosion in a flat
in the adjoining tenement on 3 May 2021. All of the flats were evacuated as
there were concerns about whether the structure of the building was safe. The
appellant lost his tenant.  Thereafter the building in which the dwelling was
situated was surrounded by secure fencing and the door to the dwelling itself
had a security door placed over it.  The appellant was unsure when the structure
of the building was deemed safe.  After any issues over the safety of the
tenement where the appellant’s dwelling is situated were resolved the
respondent continued to deny him access to the dwelling. The respondent
however, had access to the flats in the tenement owned by them and were
renovating them. By the time the appellant  was allowed access to his dwelling
on 24 October 2022 the respondent’s flats in the tenement (of which he thought
there were three in number) had been renovated and were capable of
inhabitation. The appellant was aware that at least one tenant of the respondent
had taken up occupation of a flat in the tenement on the 24 October 2022.
21.
The appellant’s position was that if the property was not capable of being
occupied it could not be said to be unoccupied. It was not unoccupied through
his choice or fault. When he managed to get back into the property, given the
circumstances of its sudden evacuation and the fact it had lain empty and

5

unheated for almost 18 months it required major repair work to render it
habitable. He was unable to start that work until after 24 October 2022. The
work was not completed until February 2023. The property was then marketed
for sale from 21 February 2023 and as a consequence the surcharge ended on
20 February 2023. He should be entitled to the dwellings under repair
exemption from 24 October 2022 being the date the dwelling was able to be
occupied and from when he was able to undertake the major repair work to
render it habitable.
The respondent
22.
Mr Robertson for the respondent relied on the respondent’s letter to the tribunal
dated 25 April, 2023 which set out the background.  He was not able to provide
the tribunal with information as to on what basis occupation of the dwelling was
prohibited by law apart from stating it was for “health and safety reasons.” The
initial exemption for a property under repair had been changed to dwelling
empty under statute meaning the exemption ran until 23 October rather than 2
May 2022. Once the exemption under para 7 of schedule 1 of the 1997 Order
(dwellings empty under statute) no longer applied the respondent considered
whether any other exemptions might apply.
23.
The exemption under para 2 of schedule 1 of the 1997 Order (Dwellings under
repair) can only apply where no more than 12 months has elapsed since the
last occupation day. He referred to the definition of “the last occupation day in
regulation 2 of the 1997 Order. The definition is that “the last occupation day”
with respect to an unoccupied dwelling means the day on which the dwelling
concerned was last occupied.” The definition was not qualified. It does not seek
to exclude from the calculation of the 12 month period any period where the
dwelling was exempt by virtue of paragraph 7. Had that been the intention of
the legislature it would have been provided for. The respondent had exercised
its powers in terms of the 2013 regulations and its policy as approved by their
Executive Committee on 21 November 2018. The policy was that after the 12
month exemption for properties under repair had expired a discount of 50% of
the council tax was allowed for a period of up to 6 months, the maximum period
allowed by statute; and thereafter an increased amount of council tax of 100%
was payable where a dwelling had been unoccupied for more than 12 months.
The 2013 Regulations allowed for only a 50% discount for 6 months after the12
month exemption had ended. That policy had been properly applied.
Findings and Reasons
24.
It is very unfortunate, if not unfair on the appellant, that whilst the respondent
prevented him from having access to his dwelling they took access to theirs in

6

the same tenement and renovated them. It would no doubt have been
convenient and expedient to the respondent and those who were renovating
the respondent’s properties to have the whole site secured during the
renovations but whether that would be a proper basis to deny the appellant
access to his dwelling is another matter. The respondent appears to taken the
fact that the properties had been evacuated as an opportunity to renovate their
properties. If this is so, then not only did the appellant potentially lose out on
rental income that might have been achieved, he was further penalised by
having the surcharge added to his council tax for not having completed, within
12 months, the required major repair work to render his dwelling habitable when
it was the respondent who had prevented his from so doing.
25.
The appellant raised his concerns in his email to the respondent of 20 May 2022
and in particular the fact that renovation work was extending the duration of the
works and thus extending the time he was being denied access. The
respondent’s reply of 24 May 2022 rehearsed what the appellant already knew
about the exemption and discount. That reply did not address the appellant’s
concern about him being denied access to allow him to carry out work. He was
advised to contact his insurance company but any costs or losses he may have
incurred would likely have been as a consequence of the respondent deciding
to renovate their properties rather than as a result of the explosion.
26.
However, these are not matters this tribunal can resolve and the appellant will
need to look elsewhere in order to ascertain if he as a right of relief against the
respondent. All the tribunal can do is review the decision of the respondent.
The question for the tribunal is was the respondent correct in allowing only a
discount against council tax of 50% from 24 October to 2 November 2022 and
thereafter applying an increased amount of council tax of 100% from 2
November 2022 rather than allowing a dwelling under repair exemption in terms
of para. 2 of schedule 1 of the 1997 Order from 24 October 2022.
27.
The dwelling under repair exemption can only apply where no more than 12
months have elapsed since the last occupation day. The 1997 order states that
“the last occupation day” with respect to an unoccupied dwelling means the day
on which the dwelling concerned was last occupied. For the appellant to
succeed the last occupation day would have to be defined as the last day it was
capable to being occupied or provide that any period where occupation of it was
prohibited by law should be excluded when calculating the 12 month limit for a
dwelling under repair exemption.
28.
The 2013 Regulations refer to an “unoccupied dwelling” as a dwelling which is
no one's sole or main residence, but which is not a second home. In the English
equivalent order (the Council Tax (Exempt Dwellings) Order 1992) an

7

“unoccupied dwelling” is a dwelling in which no one lives. The dwelling was last
occupied 3 May 2021. No one had lived in it from that date.  The result of this
is that 3 May 2021 is the starting date that the respondent was required to look
to in assessing whether a dwelling under repair exemption could be allowed.
As more than 12 months had elapsed since the last occupation day the dwelling
could not be exempt under this provision.  The 6 month discounted charge of
50% is similarly calculated by reference to the last occupation date and so could
only have extended to 2 November 2022.
29.
The respondent’s power contained in the 2013 Regulations to modify the
amount of council tax liability is limited so that the maximum amount of council
tax liability may not exceed an increase of 100%. The respondent’s policy was
to apply the maximum increase. That is amount they have applied in terms of
their policy. In reaching the decision that it did the respondent has taken into
account all of the relevant facts and circumstances and has properly applied its
own policy and the legislation by which it is bound.
Decision

30.
The appeal is refused.

Right of Appeal

31.
In terms of Section 46 of the Tribunal (Scotland) Act 2014, a party
aggrieved by the decision of the Tribunal may appeal to the Upper
Tribunal for Scotland on a point of law only. Before an appeal can be made
to the Upper Tribunal, the party must first seek permission to appeal from
the First-tier Tribunal. That party must seek permission to appeal within
30 days of the date the decision was sent to them.

title: FTS/LTC/CT/23/00029: Ms Jill Connell v South Lanarkshire Council
text:
Decision of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) under
Section 17 of the First-tier Tribunal for Scotland Local Taxation Chamber Rules
of Procedure 2022 (‘The Procedure Rules) and section 81 of the Local
Government Finance Act 1992 in relation to a Council Tax Finance/Non List
appeal against a decision of a Local Authority.

Chamber Ref:  FTS/LTC/CT/23/00029

Re:
61 Main Street, Carnwath, Lanark, ML11 8JU (“the Property”)

Parties:
Ms Jill Connell, 77 Main Street, Carnwath, Lanark, ML11 8HH (“the Appellant”)

South Lanarkshire Council, Benefits & Revenue Services, PO Box 3591,
Glasgow, G73 9ED (“the Local Authority”)

The First-tier Tribunal for Scotland (Local Taxation Chamber) (“the Tribunal”)

Tribunal Member: Nicola Irvine (Legal Member)

1. Background

1.1
The Appellant appealed the decision of the Local Authority in respect of two
applications. The first application was for exemption from paying council tax
due to the property being unoccupied and unfurnished. The second application
was for a 50% discount from council tax on the basis that the property was a
dwelling under repair.

1.2
In terms of section 81(1) of the Local Government Finance Act 1992, the
Appellant is entitled to appeal to the Tribunal if she is aggrieved by any decision
of a local authority that a dwelling is a chargeable dwelling, or that she is liable
to pay council tax in respect of such a dwelling. The Appellant was notified in
writing by the Local Authority that it believed that her grievance was not well
founded. The section 81 conditions have been met.

2. Documents lodged with the Tribunal

2.1
Letter from the Local Authority dated 25 April 2023.
2.2
Undated letter from the Appellant to the Local Authority requesting exemption
application.
2.3
Application for exemption from paying council tax due to the property being
unoccupied/unfurnished.

2.4
Copy council tax notice issued by the Local Authority to the Appellant in respect
of a different property.
2.5
Correspondence between the parties.
2.6
Application for 50% discount from council tax due to the property being under
repair/empty/awaiting demolition.
2.7
Estimates in respect of proposed work at the property and photographs of the
property.

3. Consideration of the Appeal

3.1 The parties agreed that a hearing was not required and that the appeal could be
dealt with by written representations. The Tribunal determined that it is appropriate
to dispose of the Appeal by written representations in terms of rule 9(3) of the
Procedure Rules. The issue before the Tribunal was whether an exemption should
be applied to the Property and whether a 50% discount in council tax should be
applied to the Property.

4. Findings in fact

4.1
The Appellant bought the property on 27 July 2022.
4.2
The property has been unoccupied since 31 May 2019.
4.3
On 29 August 2022 the Appellant made an application for unoccupied and
unfurnished exemption.
4.4
On 22 September 2022 the Appellant submitted a major repair application and
sought a 50% discount in council tax.
4.5
The notice of appeal was served on the Local Authority prior to 1 April 2023 and
has not been withdrawn or otherwise disposed of.

5.
Decision with reasons

5.1
The Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

5.2
The onus in a council tax appeal rests on the Appellant. The Appellant did not
set out grounds of appeal but rather indicated that she did not agree with the
Local Authority’s decision and advised that she wished to appeal the decision.

5.3
In reaching the decision, the Tribunal separately considered the Local
Authority’s refusal of each application made by the Appellant and the relevant
legislation.

5.4
In relation to the application for exemption from council tax as the Property was
unoccupied and unfurnished, the Appellant did not dispute that the Property
had been unoccupied since 31 May 2019. Schedule 1 of The Council Tax
Exempt Dwellings (Scotland) Order 1997 as amended by The Council Tax
Exempt Dwellings (Scotland) Amendment (No.2) Order 1999 sets out which
dwellings are exempt from council tax. Paragraph 2 defines an unoccupied
dwelling as that which is undergoing or has undergone major repair or structural
alteration in respect of which no more than 12 months have elapsed since the
last occupation date. Given that there was no dispute that the Property had
been unoccupied since 31 May 2019, the exemption cannot apply.
